title: Same Forecasts, Different Portfolios: Factor Normalization and Regularization
section: 7 How it relates to prior work
text:
7 How it relates to prior work
One literature estimates factor models from many characteristics; another regularises risk estimates for portfolio choice. This paper studies the step between, where a factor model’s forecast and risk become a portfolio.









Prior work
What it established
What this paper adds




Kelly et al. (2019)
Characteristics instrument time-varying factor loadings (IPCA); a zero intercept is not rejected once several hidden factors are included
The normalisation IPCA leaves free sets the units of any factor-covariance penalty; the intercept is used as a portfolio input, a different question from their test (Section V.C, p. 31)


Jagannathan and Ma (2003); Ledoit and Wolf (2004); Ledoit and Wolf (2017)
Portfolio constraints and shrinkage act as covariance regularisation and can improve portfolio selection
A constant on factor variances is a stock-level penalty whose size depends on the normalisation unless it is written in one set of units; shrinkage toward the identity inherits the dependence


Lettau and Pelger (2020)
Risk-premium PCA extracts factors that also fit average returns
Under one rule, its 0.80 lead over plain-ruler IPCA at the reference penalty is −0.08 without the penalty: the comparison measures the penalty (Table II, p. 24)


Kelly et al. (2023)
Portfolios built from signals can separate alpha from factor exposure
The intercept portfolio draws most of its return from outside the factor block without an explicit hedge, and is not factor-neutral (loading 0.45; Table V, p. 38)




A Sharpe ratio of 2.5 sits beside Kelly, Pruitt and Su’s finding that this model’s intercept cannot be distinguished from zero, and the two answer different questions. Their test asks whether the intercept loadings, one per characteristic, are jointly large; the portfolio asks whether the intercept summed across some two thousand stocks, weighted by the inverse risk matrix, has a mean per unit of risk. The second can be large when the first is not (Section V.C, p. 31).
Geometric Framework and Characteristic-Space Metrics show that the ruler decides how a fit is split without changing the fit. This paper takes its characteristic ruler from Characteristic-Space Metrics and its intercept fit, NA-IPCA, from Geometric Framework (footnote 3, p. 10), and follows a change of the ruler’s units into a portfolio: it matters only through a penalty written in those units. The Ruler Matters measures the same ruler on the stocks, and asks which familiar positions a model’s factors represent and what hedging them requires.
Interpreting Pricing Errors and Same Forecasts, Different Portfolios both ask what the model’s leftover is worth, but in different settings. The first shrinks one characteristic-based model’s alpha component (keeps an estimated fraction of it) to make forecasts more accurate under squared-error loss. The second adds the NA-IPCA intercept to expected returns inside one fitted model and measures a portfolio Sharpe ratio before trading costs. The models, objectives and samples differ, so neither result confirms or contradicts the other.
The tools are known. What is new is a check and a measurement: whether holdings move when only the units of a fixed factor penalty change, with the map that removes the dependence, and how using the full fitted mean changes a portfolio’s sensitivity to the same penalty (p. 8). It is a check, not a new estimator.

title: Same Forecasts, Different Portfolios: Factor Normalization and Regularization
text:
8 Scope

Before trading costs unless stated. The net figures charge 25 bp per dollar traded on purchases plus sales, a proportional cost that omits price impact, financing, short-sale fees and capacity (footnote 23, p. 40). The results are conditional evidence on model-based allocation, not a verified implementable trading strategy: a stock enters a month only when its next-month return is recorded, and the point-in-time availability of the characteristics is not independently verified (p. 7; footnote 7, p. 16).
Pointwise intervals. Intervals hold the rolling fits fixed and are not joint across penalties or portfolios. The 594-month sample and the plain intercept portfolio as the main-text rule were chosen after both samples and both rules were computed, and the intervals do not adjust for that (footnote 2, p. 6; footnote 12, p. 20). On all 618 months, the corresponding difference between the rulers, 0.27, has an interval that includes zero (footnote 1, p. 4; Table IA.E.6, p. IA-29).
One model, not model families. Proposition 1 maps two normalisations of one model; it says how to carry a penalty across them, not what its strength should be, and it does not equate model families, whose forecasts differ (pp. 4, 13).
The intercept is not shown to be mispricing. It is the part of the fitted mean that the factor block does not absorb; whether it reflects pricing errors, omitted factors or conditional dynamics is not imposed, and its alpha is a residual relative to the stated regressors (pp. 5–7; footnote 18, p. 27).
No best ruler or penalty. The ranking of the two rulers is a function of the penalty, and the fit cannot select the penalty (pp. 13, 23). In this sample no shrinkage of the factor covariance is needed; the design rule that does not depend on the sample is to write any penalty in stock units (p. 26).

title: Research
text:
My research asks which parts of a factor model’s answer (its factors, its alphas, its portfolios) reflect information in the data, and which reflect only how the model measures that information.
Each paper holds everything else fixed, changes one choice, and asks what moves. Read in the order below, they go from choosing the ruler, to reading the model’s alpha (the part of expected return its factors leave unexplained), to the holdings an investor ends up with.
Short on time? Start with the job market paper.

Job market paper



Job market paper
Working paper · October 2026


Question 5 of 5: Same target, different stocks?

The Ruler Matters: Factor Exposures, Attribution, and Portfolio Risk
Same target, different stocks: a factor model that fits returns better need not represent the positions an investor cares about, and whether a hedge removes the model’s factor loadings depends on the ruler that measures them. Expanding the library from 36 to 153 characteristics raises in-sample fit, yet the model’s loadings then represent momentum and size positions less fully; hedging a value position with the plain ruler leaves, on average, 46.10% of the hedged position, by squared stock weight, still on the model’s factor loadings (pp. 4–6).


In more detail

The paper measures the characteristic ruler directly on the stocks, as the cross-sectional second moment of their characteristics (Section I.A, p. 3), and asks how much of a familiar position (book-to-market, momentum, larger-firm size) an estimated loading space from instrumented principal component analysis (IPCA) can reproduce. With three latent factors and six observed ones (market, size, value, profitability, investment and momentum) held fixed, expanding the Jensen–Kelly–Pedersen library from 36 to 153 characteristics raises total stock-return R² from 17.01% to 17.70% (Table II, p. 17). The share of the momentum position that the loading space represents falls from 82.27% to 62.33%, and that of size from 90.17% to 71.93% (p. 22). Reallocating exposure shared by observed and latent factors changes their reported contributions without changing the joint fit: for size, the observed factors’ contribution rises from 1.38 to 45.53 basis points a month while the total stays at 2.16 (Section VII.A, p. 36). With the coefficients fixed, portfolios that measure exposure on the current month’s stocks rather than on each March’s have 26.62% to 69.39% lower subsequent variance at the same characteristic tilt in twelve exploratory comparisons; nine of the twelve simultaneous intervals exclude zero, and mean returns and trading do not improve uniformly (Section VI.B, pp. 32–34). The 46.10% measures how fully a hedge removes the loadings, not a reduction in return variance (p. 6).

SSRN preprint · March 2026 (preliminary version)


Question 1 of 5: Which ruler?

A Geometric Framework for Identification in Characteristic-Based Factor Models
Same data, different factors: which combinations of characteristics count as distinct depends on the ruler. The paper takes the ruler (the Gram metric) from how characteristics spread and overlap across stocks, and builds identification, no-arbitrage restrictions and inference on it.
Earlier, broader version of Characteristic-Space Metrics · grows out of the PhD thesis · listed on SSRN under the name Yang Liu.


In more detail

Take it from the data: the long-run average of how characteristics spread and overlap across stocks. The paper’s estimator, NA-IPCA, is instrumented principal component analysis (IPCA) rebuilt on that ruler. It caps how much expected return the intercept may carry; the cap is the “no-arbitrage” in the name. IPCA is the special case with the plain ruler and a cap too loose to matter. In simulations calibrated to U.S. stocks, where the true priced directions are placed by design on the combinations along which characteristics vary most, NA-IPCA recovers them (subspace distance about 0.01, on a scale from 0 for exact recovery to about 1.73 for entirely wrong directions). An IPCA benchmark with no intercept block does not (about 0.73). This design does not separate the ruler from the missing intercept block. In the paper’s efficiency and stress-test simulations, IPCA comes close as well, and the two estimators’ simulated out-of-sample fit is essentially the same.

Question 2 of 5: What does the ruler decide, and how reliable is the answer?

Characteristic-Space Metrics in Factor Models: Identification and Inference
Same fitted returns, different split: the ruler decides how returns are credited to latent factors (common drivers inferred from the data), observed factors such as the market, and an intercept (the part of expected return that no factor in the model explains). When the ruler is estimated from the data, its error belongs in the confidence intervals.
Listed on SSRN under the name Yang Liu.


In more detail

The ruler decides the split, not the fit. Models with identical fitted returns can credit them differently to latent factors, observed factors and an intercept, and R² cannot choose between them. A convention does. Because the ruler is estimated from the same data, its error belongs in the confidence intervals. In a stylised simulation built to isolate this mechanism (12 characteristics, 100 stocks, 960 time periods, 2,000 replications; not calibrated to U.S. data), nominal 95% confidence intervals (meant to contain the true value 95 times in 100) contain it only about 89–92 times in 100 when that error is left out, and about 94–95 times when it is included.

Question 3 of 5: What does a smaller alpha mean?

Interpreting Estimated Pricing Errors: Evidence from Characteristic-Based Return Forecasts
Same ruler, different target: an alpha can shrink because the factors explain more, or because the expected-return estimate they must explain (the target) has changed. Pairing each model’s estimate with each model’s factors on the same stocks, the paper finds that the large alpha gap between equal-weighted and value-weighted training mainly reflects different targets.


In more detail

In the paper’s comparison, a smaller alpha mainly reflects a change in the thing being explained, not factors that explain more. A characteristic-based model’s forecast splits into the part its factors can produce and a leftover, the alpha. The same model is trained twice, once weighting stocks equally and once by market capitalisation. Both are scored with the same ruler, on the same stocks and with the same scoring weights. The equal-weighted version’s alpha has a root-mean-square size of 117.37 basis points (hundredths of a percentage point) a month; the value-weighted version’s has 77.27. Giving the equal-weighted version only the other’s factors leaves its alpha at 116.67; giving it only the other’s expected-return estimate brings it to 75.02. Choosing the model with the smaller alpha each year adds little to forecast accuracy. Shrinking the alpha component toward zero gives more accurate forecasts than keeping it whole in 20 of 24 test settings, but more accurate than a simple average of the two models’ forecasts in only 8. The evidence is exploratory.

Question 4 of 5: Same forecast, different portfolio?

Same Forecasts, Different Portfolios: Factor Normalization and Regularization
Same forecasts, different portfolios: the small constant a portfolio rule adds to each factor’s risk is a penalty on factor bets, written in the ruler’s units, so one number gives two portfolios. Written in one set of units, or removed, the penalty gives one portfolio.


In more detail

Two versions of one IPCA fit, estimated separately under the plain and the characteristic ruler, give stock forecasts that differ by a median of 4.8 parts in a million (Table II, p. 24). With the same penalty number, their portfolios have Sharpe ratios (average excess return per unit of volatility) of 0.69 and 1.07 before trading costs over 594 months (Table I, p. 19). Written in one set of units, the penalty gives one portfolio; without it, both versions hold the same portfolio, at 1.62 (Table I, p. 19). Separately, using the full fitted mean, including the intercept the model already estimates (the part of expected return that no factor in the model explains), gives a Sharpe ratio of 2.51 before trading costs that barely moves with the penalty. Its gain over the best portfolio without an intercept is 0.89, 95% interval [0.59, 1.26], and 0.57 [0.29, 0.89] net of 25 basis points per dollar traded (Table III, p. 30). The gain weakens over time: since October 2007 its net advantage has an interval that includes zero (p. 7). This second result uses a different model, objective and sample from those in Interpreting Pricing Errors, so neither result confirms or contradicts the other.

title: Characteristic-Space Metrics in Factor Models: Identification and Inference
text:
1 The question
In the agenda, this paper follows Geometric Framework and asks: once the ruler is chosen, what does it decide, and how precisely? The next paper, Interpreting Pricing Errors, asks what a smaller alpha then means.
When a characteristic-based factor model fits returns, what decides how much of the fit it credits to latent factors, to observed factors such as the market, and to the intercept? And how precisely can that split be measured?
The model has three parts. Besides latent factors (hidden common drivers it infers from the data) and observed factors such as the market, there is the intercept: the part of expected return that no factor in this model explains (the home page’s “alpha” is a close relative, measured against a stated benchmark model). You can move part of the fit from the intercept or the market into the latent factors, adjust the latent factors to compensate, and leave every fitted return exactly as it was. Every such split fits equally well, so the fit itself cannot choose among them. A convention decides it: the ruler. Characteristics also differ in scale and overlap, even after each is standardised (Section 1, p. 2), so the choice of ruler matters.

Why a model needs a ruler. To say how much of a stock’s expected return each driver explains, a model must first decide when two combinations of characteristics are really different, and how large each one is. The rule it uses for that is the ruler. Give each characteristic a weight and add them up: every stock gets a score. Such a weighted combination is called a direction (it is not a portfolio). The plain ruler (the Euclidean or identity metric) judges a direction by its weights alone. The characteristic ruler (the Gram metric) judges it by the scores it gives real stocks: how large they typically are, and whether two directions’ scores line up across stocks, high on the same stocks and low on the same stocks. So the ruler is the convention a model uses to measure how large a direction is and how much two directions overlap. Two value signals that pick out the same cheap stocks count as overlapping under the characteristic ruler but as unrelated under the plain ruler.

title: Characteristic-Space Metrics in Factor Models: Identification and Inference
text:
2 Why it matters
When researchers report how closely the latent factors align with a benchmark, how large the intercept is, or which combinations of characteristics the latent factors represent, each number depends on the split, not only on the fit (Proposition 1, p. 7).

Economic. R² cannot tell these splits apart, so a smaller reported intercept may reflect the convention, not new explanatory power (Corollary 1, p. 7).
Statistical. The characteristic ruler (the Gram metric) is estimated from the same data. Treating it as known leaves out the ruler’s own sampling error and the way that error moves with the noise in returns (Theorem 1, p. 16); in the paper’s simulation, this makes standard errors too small (Section 8.2, p. 33). State the ruler; if it is estimated, include its error.

title: Characteristic-Space Metrics in Factor Models: Identification and Inference
text:
3 The argument at a glance


Same fit, different split. Two models can give every stock the same fitted return yet credit it differently to latent factors, observed factors and an intercept (Proposition 1, p. 7). → A simple example
The fit cannot decide. Because the fits are identical, R² and residuals cannot choose between the splits (Corollary 1, p. 7). → Why it matters
A convention decides. So the choice falls to a convention: the ruler, a metric on characteristic space (Section 3.1, pp. 6–7). → The framework
The two rulers differ in U.S. data. The characteristic ruler counts overlap by the stocks two characteristics pick out, and in U.S. characteristics (no returns used) it differs sharply from the plain ruler (Table I, p. 31). → Design and main results
Its error counts. Because this ruler is estimated from the same data, its error flows into every reported split, so the paper derives standard errors that include it and do not depend on how the model is parameterised (Theorems 1–2, pp. 16, 20). → The framework
Evidence. In a stylised simulation with 960 time periods, leaving that error out makes nominal 95% confidence intervals contain the true value only about 89–92 times in 100; including it restores coverage to about 94–95 (Table II, p. 34). → Design and main results
Near a cap. Some models, such as the Geometric Framework paper’s NA-IPCA (no-arbitrage instrumented principal component analysis, named for this cap), place a cap on intercept exposure, that is, on how much expected return the intercept may carry. When the estimate sits against that limit, the cap “binds”; below it, the cap is “slack”. The cap is measured with the same estimated ruler, so the ruler’s error moves the cap too; the paper builds a confidence interval that is valid either way, at the cost of extra width (Theorem 4, p. 29). → Design and main results

title: Characteristic-Space Metrics in Factor Models: Identification and Inference
text:
4 The framework
At each date, stock i has characteristics z_{i,t} and a next-period excess return. The model has three blocks (equation 2.1, p. 4):

r_{i,t+1} = z_{i,t}'\Gamma_\beta f_{t+1} + z_{i,t}'\Gamma_\delta g_{t+1} + z_{i,t}'\Gamma_\alpha + \varepsilon_{i,t+1}.

Here f are latent factors, g are observed factors and \Gamma_\alpha sets the intercept from characteristics. The characteristic ruler (the Gram metric) measures two directions by the scores they give real stocks (equation 2.5, p. 5):

\langle a,b\rangle_{Q_Z} = a'Q_Z\,b = \mathbb{E}\!\left[N_t^{-1}(Z_t a)'(Z_t b)\right].

The ruler “specifies a convention” for separating the blocks (p. 2): which ruler to use is declared, not discovered, but the characteristic ruler’s values are estimated from the data. The theory makes three claims.

Same fit, different split. For any ruler, a matched change normalises the latent-factor loadings, removes the other blocks’ overlap with them, and offsets both changes in the factor series, so every fitted return is unchanged (Proposition 1, p. 7). A finite cap on how much the intercept may carry is different: it is not a change of ruler, and it can exclude models and change fitted returns (pp. 2, 7).
Inference with an estimated ruler. The estimator’s large-sample linear representation adds a ruler-estimation term to the usual return-score term, including their cross-covariance (Theorem 1, p. 16). The result is one standard-error formula that includes the ruler’s own error and does not depend on how the model is parameterised (Theorem 2, p. 20).
Near an estimated cap. The estimated ruler moves the cap as well as the estimate, so in large samples the estimate behaves like a normal draw projected onto a moving boundary, and its distribution is generally not symmetric (Theorem 3, p. 26). Confidence intervals built from least-favourable (worst-case) quantiles have at least nominal coverage in large samples at any distance from the cap, and may be conservative (Theorem 4, p. 29). The guarantee excludes reports whose critical quantile sits at an atom, such as the intercept’s own size when the cap binds exactly (p. 28).



Technical statement


Target. A loading class defined up to latent-factor rotations, identified by local curvature (Proposition 2, p. 8); covariance alignment, with local regularity and a strictly slack cap, suffices to make it the structural class even with a fixed cross section (Proposition 3, p. 12).
Estimator. Exactly profiled (each date’s factors solved exactly by least squares for any candidate loadings, dates combined with fixed weights, only loadings searched), on a regular local branch (Theorem 1, p. 16).
Reports. Each smooth report has a chart-invariant influence function (Theorem 2, p. 20); HAC estimation gives valid intervals (Proposition 5, p. 23). For one constraint and a scalar report, the slack and binding endpoints suffice (Proposition 6, p. 28).

title: Characteristic-Space Metrics in Factor Models: Identification and Inference
Characteristic-Space Metrics in Factor Models: Identification and Inference
text:
6 Design and main results
The evidence has three parts (Section 8, pp. 30–38). A U.S. stock panel with 153 monthly characteristics, 1962–2025, measures how much real characteristics overlap (Section 8.1, p. 30). A stylised simulation (L = 12 characteristics, N = 100 stocks, 2,000 replications at T = 240 and 960 time periods) holds the point estimate fixed and compares ways of computing standard errors (pp. 32–33). A local experiment, a stylised simulation of the large-sample approximation that does not re-estimate a factor panel (p. 38), places the true value at set distances from an estimated cap on the intercept and compares confidence intervals near it (Section 8.3, pp. 35–36).

Measured by the stocks they pick out, 68 suffice (Table I, p. 31). How to read it. Rows are ways of computing standard errors (Table II, p. 34); circles and squares are two reported quantities, each measuring how closely a fixed combination of characteristics aligns with the span of the latent factors (true value 0.5). The top two rows (“Monte Carlo scale”, “Oracle-influence HAC”) are infeasible benchmarks: they need information available only in a simulation. Compare “Ruler treated as known” with “Complete-score HAC” (HAC: heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent), the paper’s full method, which includes the ruler’s error. The dashed line is the target: nominal 95% coverage (intervals that contain the true value 95 times in 100), or standard errors equal to the Monte Carlo standard deviation across replications. “Tail calibration” compares quantiles of the standardised estimate with normal quantiles at T = 960; the dashed grey diagonal is a perfect fit. Source: paper Table II and Figure 2, and Section 8.2 for the paired gains; rebuilt_interior_coverage.csv, paired_coverage_gains.csv, studentized_quantiles.csv. Data



What this shows. With 960 time periods, treating the estimated ruler as known makes standard errors too small, so nominal 95% confidence intervals contain the true value only about 89 and 92 times in 100. Including the ruler’s error restores coverage to about 94–95; the paired coverage gains, 5.20 and 3.10 percentage points, have Monte Carlo standard errors of 0.50 and 0.39 (Table II, p. 34). Most of the shortfall is the ruler’s own variance (Section 8.2, p. 33); with 240 time periods even the complete and oracle methods fall slightly short, at about 93–94 times, from finite-sample error in estimating the long-run (HAC) covariance (p. 33).

Near an estimated cap, the paper’s stylised local experiment (960 time periods) again targets nominal 95% confidence intervals. One calibrated as if the cap binds contains the true value as few as about 84 times in 100 (83.80%) when the cap is in fact slack. One that holds whether or not the cap binds (the paper’s drift-robust interval) contains it about 96–99 times (96.30–98.75%) at every tested distance (Table III, p. 36). The price is width: when the cap binds, it is about 25% wider (3.241 against 2.584) than an infeasible benchmark that knows how far the true value sits from the cap, which no one can compute in practice (Table III, p. 36).

title: Characteristic-Space Metrics in Factor Models: Identification and Inference
section: 7 How it relates to prior work
text:
7 How it relates to prior work
Factor-model inference usually fixes rotation and scale by a normalisation. This paper asks what that normalisation does to the split when the ruler behind it is estimated from the data.









Prior work
What it established
What this paper adds




Bai (2003); Bai and Ng (2013)
Identification and inference for large approximate factor models under normalisation restrictions.
Loadings identified up to latent-factor rotations for each ruler (metric), keeping observed-factor and intercept blocks; theory for a fixed cross section.


Kelly et al. (2019)
IPCA: characteristics instrument each stock’s loadings (betas) on latent factors, with an intercept and optional observed factors; rotation is fixed with the plain ruler, Γβ′Γβ = I.
Treats that normalisation as one choice of ruler, shows the split depends on it, and carries an estimated characteristic ruler (Gram metric) into inference.


Newey (1994); Newey and McFadden (1994); Andrews and Guggenberger (2009); Andrews and Soares (2010)
First-step estimation corrections; uniformly valid inference when inequality constraints may bind.
Applies the two-step correction to a ruler that both selects the split and enters the report; near one smooth cap, uniform intervals from two endpoint calculations.




The angle is measurement, not a new predictor. The tools are known: geometry on matrix manifolds, two-step adjustment and constrained projection. What is new is their combination for one object, a split of fitted returns whose ruler is estimated from the same data and may also set the cap on the intercept.


For specialists: further related work

Matrix-manifold geometry (Edelman et al. 1998) removes latent-factor rotations; boundary limit laws (Geyer 1994; Andrews 1999; Shapiro 2000) are extended to a boundary learned through the same ruler; and where Li (2025) bootstraps constrained estimators, this paper’s route is analytic and uniform over local slack.

Where it fits. Geometric Framework, an earlier and broader version of this paper, argued for taking the ruler from the data; this paper proves that the ruler decides how a fixed fit is split and shows how to do inference when the ruler is estimated. Same Forecasts, Different Portfolios cites it for the characteristic ruler (the Gram metric) (footnote 3, p. 10) and follows a change of the ruler’s units into a portfolio; Interpreting Pricing Errors cites it for the representation identities (p. 4) and holds the ruler fixed to read alphas. The Ruler Matters measures the same characteristic ruler month by month on the stocks, and asks which familiar positions a model’s factors represent and what hedging them requires.

title: Same fit, different attribution
text: Measured · Project · research evidence · June 2026 · sources: seminar deck When Geometry Matters (24 June 2026) and report Statistical Factor Models Carry a Hidden Ruler (27 June 2026) · All projects

title: Same fit, different attribution
text:
The setting 
A factor model used for risk or return attribution splits expected return between the factors and the intercept, the part that no factor in this model explains. To make that split, the model needs a ruler: formally, a metric (an inner product) on characteristic space. Weighting the characteristics and adding them up gives every stock a score; such a weighted sum is a direction (not a portfolio). The ruler measures how large a direction is and how much two directions overlap. The plain ruler (the Euclidean or identity metric) judges a direction by its weights alone. The characteristic ruler (the Gram metric) judges it by the scores it gives real stocks. Standard implementations use the plain ruler without saying so. On 153 U.S. characteristics, switching rulers leaves the fit alone and moves the split, so a change of risk or attribution model can move reported factor attributions without any new information.

title: Same fit, different attribution
text:
Exhibit 1: 153 characteristics, far fewer directions 
 (opens the full-size image in a new tab)Share of the characteristics’ total variation captured by the directions that vary most under the characteristic ruler (blue; Q_Z in the chart is the characteristic Gram matrix, and its principal components (PCs) are the directions), against 153 equally large directions (grey). Ruler averaged over January 1962 to November 2025, so the curve describes the library, not what a model could have known at the time. Source: seminar deck When Geometry Matters, slide 17.

Key takeaway. 42 directions account for about 80% of the variation and 67 to 68 for 90%, depending on the months used (report, p. 2): the library overlaps heavily, so how overlap is measured (the choice of metric) is a real modelling choice. These are directions of variation in the characteristics, not priced risks.

title: Universes, trading costs and backtest checks
text: Measured · Project · research evidence · July 2026 · source: institutional research brief Adaptive Characteristic Geometry in Systematic Equity Portfolios (10 July 2026) · All projects

title: Universes, trading costs and backtest checks
text:
The setting 
Two questions matter before any model reaches a book: does its advantage hold across stock-size universes, and how sensitive is it to trading costs? A research brief answers both descriptively on one rolling-window protocol: 618 months, June 1973 to November 2024, with positions scaled each month to a gross exposure (long plus short) of one. IPCA (instrumented principal component analysis, a standard characteristic-based factor model) uses the plain ruler (the Euclidean or identity metric). QZ-IPCA changes only the ruler, to the characteristic ruler (the Gram metric). NA-IPCA uses the characteristic ruler and adds the intercept (the part of expected return that no factor in the model explains), with a cap on how much it may carry.

title: Universes, trading costs and backtest checks
section: Exhibit 1: Where across universes the models differ
text:
Exhibit 1: Where across universes the models differ 
 (opens the full-size image in a new tab)Differences against IPCA, gross of trading costs: Sharpe ratio (left) and maximum drawdown in percentage points, higher = shallower (right). “NA-IPCA (alpha-aware)” uses the intercept without the risk adjustment. The Micro universe appears only in this brief; the later evidence report and Same Forecasts, Different Portfolios exclude micro caps. Source: brief Adaptive Characteristic Geometry in Systematic Equity Portfolios, Figure 1, p. 3.

Key takeaway. NA-IPCA with its intercept has a higher Sharpe ratio than IPCA in all five universes, with the smallest gap among mega caps (+0.64). It changes the ruler (metric) and adds the intercept at once, so the gap is not the intercept’s value alone. QZ-IPCA, which changes only the ruler, is ahead in the broad Core universe (+0.37) and behind among mega and micro caps (−0.09 and −0.43). In Same Forecasts, Different Portfolios’s same-fit comparison, the intercept’s mean-return gain is statistically significant in all four universes over 1975–2024 (every 95% interval excludes zero) but in none since October 2007 (Table IA.I.3, p. IA-46). The drawdown panel compares books of equal gross exposure, not equal volatility: in Core, NA-IPCA runs at 3.1% annualised volatility against 6.1% for IPCA (brief, Table 1, p. 2), so part of its shallower drawdown is lower risk.

title: Universes, trading costs and backtest checks
section: Exhibit 2: Cost thresholds under a turnover proxy
text:
Exhibit 2: Cost thresholds under a turnover proxy 
 (opens the full-size image in a new tab)Sharpe ratio of the return after a proxy cost (gross return minus the assumed one-way charge times proxy turnover), recomputed at every charge; Core universe, 618 months. Proxy turnover is each month’s raw turnover divided by that month’s book size, not trades reconstructed from holdings. RP-PCA = risk-premium principal component analysis, another factor model. Source: brief Adaptive Characteristic Geometry in Systematic Equity Portfolios, Figure 2, p. 3.

Key takeaway. Under the proxy, the average return falls to zero at a one-way charge of 87 bp (basis points; 1 bp = 0.01 percentage point) for IPCA, 115 for QZ-IPCA, 137 for NA-IPCA with the intercept and 146 for RP-PCA. The intercept rule has higher turnover, so above roughly 130 bp RP-PCA has the highest Sharpe ratio after the proxy cost. These are sensitivity thresholds, not implementable break-even costs: on its 594-month sample, Same Forecasts, Different Portfolios charges a cost on every dollar bought or sold, computed from the portfolio weights, and reports break-even costs of 68 bp for the intercept portfolio and 70 for RP-PCA; its costs are proportional only, with no price impact, financing, short-sale fees or capacity (Table IV, p. 35; p. 7).

title: From forecast to portfolio
text:
The setting 
Nearly identical forecasts can give different portfolios, and each backtest’s book size is a by-product of estimation. How should models be compared? Core stocks (U.S. stocks excluding micro caps) are described by 132 characteristics; models are refitted monthly on the previous 120 months, and one mean–variance rule forms each month’s long–short portfolio: 618 months, June 1973 to November 2024. IPCA (instrumented principal component analysis, a standard characteristic-based factor model) uses the plain ruler (the Euclidean metric); QZ-IPCA switches to the characteristic ruler (the Gram metric); NA-IPCA also estimates a capped intercept, the part of expected return that no factor in this model explains.

title: From forecast to portfolio
section: Exhibit 1: The forecasts agree in every month
text:
Exhibit 1: The forecasts agree in every month 
 (opens the full-size image in a new tab)Relative difference between the separately estimated IPCA and QZ-IPCA forecast vectors across 618 months, log scale. QZ-IPCA: exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) version of the characteristic ruler (Same Forecasts, Different Portfolios, p. 17). Source: NA-IPCA Methodology and Evidence Report, Figure 3, p. 6.

Key takeaway. The two forecasts differ by a median of 4.7 parts in a million, at most 1.4 in ten thousand. Yet over the same 618 months, Same Forecasts, Different Portfolios reports a typical weight similarity of 0.83 for the two portfolios (1 = identical proportions, 0 = no overlap; Table IA.D.2, p. IA-19). The gap traces to a small fixed constant (a penalty) added to each factor’s risk in the units of the ruler (the metric); written in one set of units, or removed, it leaves the weights essentially identical (Table II, p. 24). Neither ruler is claimed to give the better risk model.

Key takeaway. The complete intercept rule separates NA-IPCA from every factor-only portfolio (Sharpe ratio 2.49 against 0.32 without it), but every slope falls after the late 2000s: from October 2007 (206 months), 1.12 against 0.16 (Table 4). Same Forecasts, Different Portfolios tests the same 206 months on average return: among Core stocks, the complete rule (the paper’s stabilized intercept portfolio) earns 0.20 percentage points a month more than the same fit without the intercept, 95% interval [−0.07, 0.41], p = 0.11 (Table IA.I.3, p. IA-46). On the paper’s 594 months from June 1975, its Sharpe ratio falls from 3.97 to 3.03 to 1.13 across three 198-month thirds (Internet Appendix IA.G.2, p. IA-34).

title: From forecast to portfolio
text:
Where this connects

title: Building the characteristic ruler
text:
The setting 
A model that uses the characteristic ruler has to estimate it: the characteristic Gram matrix, whose entries are products of characteristics averaged across stocks and over an estimation window (the characteristics’ second moments). The raw average keeps the data’s overlap structure but can be numerically unstable, because a few directions vary far more than others. The condition number measures this: the ratio of the matrix’s largest to smallest eigenvalue, that is, the variation of the direction that varies most divided by that of the direction that varies least, where 1 means all directions are equally large. Risk teams routinely stabilise such matrices, by shrinkage, by eigenvalue filtering (keeping only the directions that vary most), or by weighting recent months more. This report keeps the estimation method fixed and changes only how the characteristic ruler is built. There are seven versions: the raw average; shrinkage of 5%, 10% or 20% toward a rescaled plain ruler (a scaled identity matrix, the Euclidean metric); the 40 directions that vary most (the leading eigenvectors), with a small floor on the rest; a 36-month exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA); and EWMA plus the 40-direction filter. The baseline is IPCA (instrumented principal component analysis, a standard factor model in which characteristics set each stock’s factor exposures) with the plain ruler.

Exhibit 1: Cross-sectional R² against numerical conditioning

Chart labels: raw = raw average of the characteristic Gram matrix; PCA 40 = the 40 directions that vary most (leading principal components); EWMA+PCA = EWMA plus the 40-direction filter. Key takeaway. The raw average has the highest out-of-sample cross-sectional R² (0.458) but the highest condition number (2,963). Shrinking it by 5% keeps 0.440 at 325.5; the 36-month EWMA falls to 0.259. Because this statistic leaves out the intercept, a higher value means more of expected return is credited to the factors, not a better-fitting model (Exhibit 2). The choice is a trade-off between keeping the data’s overlap structure and numerical stability.

Figure 1 shows what the characteristic ruler measures and the plain ruler assumes away: how much eight related characteristics overlap across stocks, re-estimated each month from 1983 to 2025.1 The next section explains what a ruler is, and why switching rulers changes how returns are split between factors and the part no factor explains, and what an investor holds.

title: Mingyang Liu
text:
Research agenda

Same information, different answer: before trusting what a factor model says, check its ruler.

A factor model explains many stocks’ returns with a few common drivers. Built on stock characteristics (size, value, momentum and many more), it gives three answers: which risks are priced, how much expected return its factors leave unexplained (the alpha), and what to hold. I ask how much of each answer comes from information in the data, and how much from choices that add no information. The central choice is the ruler. To credit a stock’s expected return to its drivers, a model must first decide when two combinations of characteristics are really different and how large each one is. The rule it uses for that is the ruler: technically, a metric (an inner product) on characteristic space. I estimate the ruler from the data. I show that changing it changes how returns are split between the factors and the part no factor explains (the intercept; the alpha is a close relative, measured against a stated benchmark model), but not how well they are fitted, and I carry the ruler’s own estimation error into the confidence intervals. I then ask what a smaller alpha really reflects, and how the ruler, and the library of characteristics it measures, change what an investor holds. Researchers and portfolio managers change such conventions routinely, and a change of convention is easy to mistake for a discovery.

Give each characteristic a weight and add them up: every stock gets a score. Such a weighted combination is called a direction (it is not a portfolio). The plain ruler (the Euclidean or identity metric) judges a direction by its weights alone. The characteristic ruler (the Gram metric) judges it by the scores it gives real stocks: how large they typically are, and whether two directions’ scores line up across stocks, high on the same stocks and low on the same stocks.
The ruler is the convention a model uses to measure how large a direction is and how much two directions overlap. Two value signals that pick out the same cheap stocks count as overlapping under the characteristic ruler but as unrelated under the plain ruler.

title: Mingyang Liu
text:
Research


SSRN preprint · March 2026 (preliminary version)

A Geometric Framework for Identification in Characteristic-Based Factor Models
Same data, different factors: which combinations of characteristics count as distinct depends on the ruler. The paper takes the ruler (the Gram metric) from how characteristics spread and overlap across stocks, and builds identification, no-arbitrage restrictions and inference on it.
Earlier, broader version of Characteristic-Space Metrics.
Paper page · PDF · SSRN



SSRN preprint · September 2026

Characteristic-Space Metrics in Factor Models: Identification and Inference
Same fitted returns, different split: the ruler decides how returns are credited to latent factors (common drivers inferred from the data), observed factors such as the market, and an intercept. When the ruler is estimated from the data, its error belongs in the confidence intervals.
Paper page · PDF · SSRN



Working paper · September 2026

Interpreting Estimated Pricing Errors: Evidence from Characteristic-Based Return Forecasts
Same ruler, different target: an alpha can shrink because the factors explain more, or because the expected-return estimate they must explain (the target) has changed. Pairing each model’s estimate with each model’s factors on the same stocks, the paper finds that the large alpha gap between equal-weighted and value-weighted training mainly reflects different targets.
Paper page · PDF



Working paper · October 2026

Same Forecasts, Different Portfolios: Factor Normalization and Regularization
Same forecasts, different portfolios: the small constant a portfolio rule adds to each factor’s risk is a penalty on factor bets, written in the ruler’s units, so one number gives two portfolios. With the same number, two versions of one model that forecast alike have Sharpe ratios (average excess return per unit of volatility) of 0.69 and 1.07 before trading costs (Table I, p. 19). Written in one set of units, or removed, the penalty gives one portfolio.
Paper page · Paper (PDF)



Working paper · October 2026

The Ruler Matters: Factor Exposures, Attribution, and Portfolio Risk
Same target, different stocks: a factor model that fits returns better need not represent the positions an investor cares about, and whether a hedge removes the model’s factor loadings depends on the ruler that measures them. Expanding the library from 36 to 153 characteristics raises in-sample fit, yet the model’s loadings then represent momentum and size positions less fully; hedging a value position with the plain ruler leaves, on average, 46.10% of the hedged position, by squared stock weight, still on the model’s factor loadings (pp. 4–6).
Paper page · Paper (PDF)



Research in progress. Exposure or Intercept? Identifying Corporate Bond Premia with No-Arbitrage IPCA, with Paolo Zaffaroni (in preparation). An ongoing research collaboration with Prof. Semyon Malamud (EPFL and Swiss Finance Institute) on portfolio construction from linear out-of-sample return forecasts. See Research in progress.

text: Characteristics: the Jensen–Kelly–Pedersen library of 153 U.S. stock characteristics (JKP153), the same library that The Ruler Matters uses, each characteristic rank-centred within the month and signed so that the trait named in the row scores high. Each window averages, with equal weights, the monthly 153×153 second-moment matrices of these characteristics over the 240 months ending in the month shown. Window ends run from June 1983 to November 2025. There are 510 windows, and no future months enter any window. The 240-month equal-weighted window is this exhibit’s own choice. Same Forecasts, Different Portfolios reports the rolling-60, equal-120 and EWMA (exponentially weighted moving average) versions of the characteristic ruler (p. 17), and the path depends on the window. The table takes the 8×8 block for market equity (sign reversed), Amihud illiquidity, turnover (reversed), idiosyncratic volatility, a distress score (Ohlson O-score), debt to market equity, operating profitability (reversed) and firm age (reversed), and rescales it to unit diagonals, so the cells are approximately correlations. The block is a chosen high-overlap corner of the library, not a representative sample; summaries of the overlaps among all 153 characteristics are in Characteristic-Space Metrics, Table I (p. 31) and Figure 1 (p. 32). The most overlapping pair is small size and illiquidity in every window; Amihud illiquidity is built from dollar volume, so a large overlap with size is expected. Accounting inputs change only when new financial statements are filed, and coverage, the share of missing values and the stock universe change over time; those changes move these averages as well as any change in how firms line up. The participation dimension in the timeline is computed from the full 153×153 window matrix, not from the 8×8 block, and runs from 21.7 to 22.9. This is a descriptive visualisation, not a new estimator or causal test.↩︎

Characteristic-Space Metrics in Factor Models: Identification and Inference
SSRN preprint, September 2026. DOI: 10.2139/ssrn.7445120
Factor models with identical fit can credit returns differently to latent factors, observed factors and an intercept; fit cannot choose the split, but the inner product chosen for characteristic space does. The paper derives rotation-invariant inference that carries the Gram metric’s estimation error, and drift-robust confidence intervals near an intercept cap (exposure budget).
PDF · Online supplement · SSRN


A Geometric Framework for Identification in Characteristic-Based Factor Models
SSRN preprint, March 2026 (preliminary version). DOI: 10.2139/ssrn.7013178. Grows out of the PhD thesis; its inference theory is developed further in Characteristic-Space Metrics.
Using a metric taken from the long-run cross-sectional distribution of firm characteristics, the paper derives NA-IPCA, which nests IPCA, caps how much the intercept may carry and admits rotation-invariant inference. In the headline calibrated simulation, NA-IPCA recovers the latent pricing span and an intercept-free IPCA benchmark does not; that design does not isolate the metric.
PDF · SSRN


Same Forecasts, Different Portfolios: Factor Normalization and Regularization
Working paper, October 2026
Two IPCA fits under different normalisations give nearly identical forecasts but different gross Sharpe ratios: a ridge added to factor covariances penalises exposures in units the normalisation sets. Writing the penalty consistently aligns the portfolios. Using the full fitted mean, intercept included, raises the gross Sharpe ratio; its net advantage since October 2007 is imprecise.

Interpreting Estimated Pricing Errors: Evidence from Characteristic-Based Return Forecasts
Working paper, September 2026
What does a smaller estimated pricing error (alpha) tell a model user? On 153 U.S. characteristics, crossing the expected-return estimates and factor spaces of one model’s equal- and value-weighted fits shows that their gap in fitted intercept magnitudes mainly reflects different estimated means; residual diagnostics add little to forecast selection (exploratory evidence).

Cite: Jensen, T. I., B. Kelly and L. H. Pedersen (2023). “Is There a Replication Crisis in Finance?” Journal of Finance 78(5), 2465–2518. doi:10.1111/jofi.13249

CRSP and Compustat, following Kelly, Pruitt and Su (2019)

Monthly stock returns from the Center for Research in Security Prices and firm accounts from S&P Global Compustat, accessed through WRDS. Geometric Framework builds its panel following the replication dataset of the paper that introduced IPCA (instrumented principal component analysis, in which characteristics serve as instruments for each stock’s time-varying factor loadings, or betas: how strongly it moves with the common factors), with its timing convention and cross-sectional rank transformation (Section 6.1, pp. 26–27). The panel has 36 characteristics plus a constant (L = 37). It covers 12,813 firms and 599 months. The sample runs from July 1964 to May 2014. Table 6 (p. 32) maps each characteristic to its WRDS/Neuhierl variable code. The Ruler Matters pairs its characteristics with CRSP monthly returns and trading status, and splits stocks into source and target groups by a fixed hash of the CRSP identifier (Section II.A, p. 9; Internet Appendix IA.2, p. 58).
Cite: Center for Research in Security Prices, University of Chicago Booth School of Business; S&P Global Compustat; both via Wharton Research Data Services. Kelly, B. T., S. Pruitt and Y. Su (2019). “Characteristics Are Covariances: A Unified Model of Risk and Return.” Journal of Financial Economics 134(3), 501–524. doi:10.1016/j.jfineco.2019.05.001

Fama–French factors and portfolios

Monthly factor returns, the risk-free rate and 25 double-sorted portfolios from Kenneth R. French’s Data Library. Same Forecasts, Different Portfolios uses the five factors as observed factors (Section III.A, pp. 16–17). The Ruler Matters uses the five factors plus momentum (FFC6) as observed factors (Section II.B, p. 11).
Cite: Fama, E. F. and K. R. French (1993). “Common Risk Factors in the Returns on Stocks and Bonds.” Journal of Financial Economics 33(1), 3–56. doi:10.1016/0304-405X(93)90023-5. Fama, E. F. and K. R. French (2015). “A Five-Factor Asset Pricing Model.” Journal of Financial Economics 116(1), 1–22. doi:10.1016/j.jfineco.2014.10.010

NBER recession dates

Peak and trough months of U.S. business cycles from the NBER Business Cycle Dating Committee. Same Forecasts, Different Portfolios shades recessions in Figure 2 (p. 23) and reports its portfolios in both business-cycle regimes (Section VI.C, p. 39); on this site they are used for shading only, in that paper’s Internet Appendix comparison figure.
Cite: National Bureau of Economic Research. “US Business Cycle Expansions and Contractions.”

title: Data & Code
text:
Research tools: data contracts
Each research tool in the Research Toolkit is demonstrated on one archived example. For each, the contract states what the function reads and writes, how far its code is tested, and what stays private. Maturity labels as on the tool pages: Implemented & tested Archived research example Planned extension.

Return-State Behavior Profile




Item
Contract




Inputs
Monthly rows: date (sorted, unique, consecutive), strategy_return and benchmark_return as decimal returns for the same months, optional cash_return; metadata on source, currency, cost convention (net or gross), last update and permission to publish. Only the benchmark defines the market states; no factor, signal or stock characteristic enters.


Configuration
Return stream (seven: four archived, three built from public market and Treasury-bill returns) and state definition (deciles 10/90 with a 5% tail; quintiles 20/80 with a 10% tail; deciles 10/90 with a −10% recovery drawdown), on the full sample only. Half-sample results are not published: they would let single months of the private stream be reconstructed from the aggregates.


Outputs
For each stream and definition: eight state-conditional metrics (raw value, units, standard error and 95% interval, normalised radar score with a clipping flag), state rule, n per state, thresholds, date range, benchmark, and a warning wherever n is below 15. A CSV export of the current view on the page; all 21 results in return_state.json.


Site file
return_state.json, behind the interactive figures on the tool page: built from the archived strategy white paper’s monthly backtest tables (2026); aggregates only.


Example
Archived systematic long–short U.S. equity strategy backtest (the white paper’s title calls it “Regime-Aware”; the portfolio rule itself has no regime switch): monthly data Apr 2007 – Nov 2025 (224 months), net of a bid-ask cost proxy charged on rebalancing months (on average 0.73 percentage points a month). The proxy excludes borrow, financing and market-impact costs; the portfolio is equal-weighted across the whole stock universe, and its capacity was not assessed. A historical backtest, not live or audited trading. The configuration was selected from several in an earlier study (selection bias not corrected), and the estimation sample of its signal loadings may overlap the backtest period, so it is not an out-of-sample result.


Code status
Implemented & tested pipeline/exhibits/return_state.py in the site’s public repository, with tests for input validation, parity with the archived radar table to within 1 × 10⁻⁸, state counts, intervals, aggregates-only output and a disclosure screen under which no single month of the private stream is exactly solvable from the published linear aggregates (an author-set heuristic limit, not a privacy guarantee). Validated on this archive only; other return streams and a different factor behind the stream are a Planned extension.


Public
The aggregates (per-state counts, thresholds and the eight metrics) and the code.


Private
The monthly return streams and the white-paper tables they come from; the upstream signal, portfolio and backtest code. None of these is published.


How to request
Hiring teams may ask at yang.liu19@imperial.ac.uk for a walkthrough of the code and its tests. Please do not send proprietary return data: this site has no secure handling for it.






Macro Forecast Evaluation & Regime Diagnostics




Item
Contract




Inputs
Per-origin forecast records: origin month, horizon, model, outcome and forecast, one record per model, origin and horizon, for a target defined once for every model; a baseline fixed in advance; monthly persistence estimates for the persistence monitor. For a new application, every predictor value needs the date on which it was first available (its vintage or release date).


Configuration
Output version, horizon, model and window (each model’s own window or the common window of all models).


Outputs
n, RMSE, MAE and direction hit rate per model; RMSE relative to the baseline; the per-origin loss differential and its running sum; Diebold–Mariano tests (equal-weight long-run variance with h − 1 lags as in the original test, Harvey–Leybourne–Newbold small-sample correction; a Newey–West (Bartlett) p-value as a sensitivity check); forecast errors split by signal state. All in forecast_eval.json.


Site file
forecast_eval.json, behind the interactive figures and table on the tool page: built from the author’s UK services-inflation runs of February 2026 and ONS data (Open Government Licence). Its meta block records the SHA-256 hash of each archived source file, the parity results and the code version.


Example
UK services inflation, February 2026 research snapshot: two archived runs (23 and 24 February 2026) and a re-estimation trained only on outcomes observed by the origin (the smoothed state, full-sample standardisation and latest-vintage data still carry look-ahead); ONS monthly data through Dec 2025 (MM23 release of 18 February 2026). Archived forecasts, not a forecasting service.


Code status
Implemented & tested pipeline/exhibits/forecast_eval.py in the site’s public repository, with unit tests on synthetic cases (including invalid input records) and parity with the archived model-comparison tables to 10⁻⁹; its expanding-window forecasting function reproduces the latest run’s stored forecasts to 10⁻¹⁰. From a clean clone of the public repository, the synthetic tests and the page-versus-JSON checks run; the parity tests need the private archive and are skipped. Archived research example data download, the state-space smoother and the rolling regressions, not rerun. Planned extension a loader for new record files; other variables, predictors and countries.


Public
The aggregates, the per-origin running sum of the loss differential, the monthly persistence estimates and the ONS CPI series (Open Government Licence v3.0), and the evaluation code.


Private
The replication folder: raw downloads, processed inputs, estimation scripts and per-origin forecast files. None of these is published.


How to request
The ONS series are public at the Office for National Statistics. For a walkthrough of the evaluation code and its tests, write to yang.liu19@imperial.ac.uk.

title: Data & Code
text:
Code
The 618 rolling windows of the intercept fit behind Same Forecasts, Different Portfolios were estimated with the two Python packages released together as NA-IPCA v1.2.0, naipca and gcde; its two zero-intercept IPCA fits ran through the separate QZ-IPCA benchmark package (v1.0.1). The same packages implement the NA-IPCA family whose theory Geometric Framework and Characteristic-Space Metrics develop. Interpreting Pricing Errors estimates characteristic-based latent-factor models with an intercept (three factors at baseline; Section 3.2, p. 9), with ridge regressions as comparison benchmarks (p. 8). The Ruler Matters estimates IPCA with three latent factors and FFC6, with and without a characteristic intercept, on 36 and 153 characteristics (Section II.B, p. 11). Same Forecasts, Different Portfolios (p. 43; package available on request), The Ruler Matters (Internet Appendix IA.2, p. 58) and Characteristic-Space Metrics (p. 38) describe their own replication packages, separate from the toolkit.

The model family
Each model has up to three blocks: latent (hidden) factors inferred from the data, observed factors and the intercept (the part of expected return that no factor in this model explains). They differ in the ruler (metric) they measure with and in what they do with the intercept.










Model
Ruler
Intercept
What it adds




IPCA (Kelly, Pruitt and Su, 2019)
the plain ruler (the Euclidean or identity metric)
optional intercept, no cap
the baseline: characteristics instrument the factor loadings (betas), that is, how strongly each stock moves with the common factors


QZ-IPCA
the characteristic ruler (the Gram metric) Q_Z, supplied (for example its exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) version)
none
the same model measured with the characteristic ruler


NA-IPCA
the characteristic ruler Q_Z, supplied
estimated jointly under the cap \Gamma_\alpha' Q_Z \Gamma_\alpha \le \delta
the intercept as a third block; the cap is the “no-arbitrage” in the name (slack, that is, non-binding, in every window of Same Forecasts, Different Portfolios)






Two packages
naipca estimates NA-IPCA by projected alternating least squares: it solves for the factors and the loading blocks in turn, projects the loadings back onto the constraint set, and stops when the fit to the characteristic-managed portfolio returns stops improving. It refuses an invalid supplied ruler at intake rather than repairing it; if a valid ruler is ill-conditioned, the solver shrinks it toward a scaled identity matrix by the smallest amount that makes it factorisable and reports that amount (QZ.lambda) in the audit record. Missing observations are handled through availability masks, never imputed.
gcde (Geometry Construction and Diagnostics Engine) builds the characteristic ruler (the Gram metric Q_Z) from the monthly Gram matrices of the characteristics and reports on it: 37 registered construction methods (counting parameter aliases) in six families (baseline, shrinkage, eigenvalue repair, adaptive conditioning, low-rank, rolling or exponentially weighted). It adds three diagnostic modules (spectrum, subspace, dynamic) and four validation labels (STABLE, WATCH, HIGH_ANISOTROPY, FAIL_NOT_SPD). Because construction and estimation are separate programs, every run records which ruler was used, built how and from which window. No construction is certified as best: a ruler is a measurement convention.


Verification and reproducibility

Verification. All thirty regression-test cases agree with a separate MATLAB reference implementation held by the author to within 2.97 × 10⁻¹⁴. All five invalid rulers (metric matrices) are rejected as designed. The solver has no random element: identical inputs give bit-identical outputs. Its defaults carry a configuration-freeze certificate and are never tuned in place. Every fit attaches an audit record: initialisation source, SHA-256 fingerprints of ruler, dataset and configuration, the stabilisation amount, convergence and runtime. The release is SHA-256 pinned, and its hash is recorded in each of the 618 estimation windows behind Same Forecasts, Different Portfolios; requesters receive the hashes with the certification package.



Rolling estimation
Rolling, expanding and online estimation are one loop: each window’s result is the next window’s warm start. A versioned state object (NAIPCAState) carries loadings, fingerprints and lineage; a warm start with the wrong dimension or factor count is rejected. The toolkit’s runtime benchmark is a small synthetic design of six overlapping windows (60 stocks, 10 characteristics, 36 months each). On it, warm starts cut solver iterations by about 55% and runtime by a factor of about 2.2 over the windows after the first. One window ran slower warm than cold. A same-window refit falls from 14 to 2 iterations.


How it is used

Build the monthly Gram matrices of the rank-transformed characteristics.
Construct the ruler (the Gram metric Q_Z) with gcde (its default averages the monthly Gram matrices; Same Forecasts, Different Portfolios uses the EWMA version, p. 17) and read its diagnostics.
Fit with naipca: data mapping, ruler, numbers of latent and observed factors, cap; read diagnostics_summary.
Roll the window with warm_start, keeping each window’s audit record.

from naipca import fit_naipca, load_frozen_config, diagnostics_summary

# D: data mapping; Q: characteristic geometry from the GCDE toolkit
config = load_frozen_config(overrides={"max_outer": 1000, "tol_outer": 1e-6})
result = fit_naipca(D, geometry={"Q": Q, "method": "raw_mean_w"},
                    K_lat=3, K_obs=5, delta=0.05, opts=config.options)
print(diagnostics_summary(result))

The quick-start sketch from the toolkit’s README. K_lat, K_obs: numbers of latent and observed factors; delta: the cap \delta in \Gamma_\alpha' Q_Z \Gamma_\alpha \le \delta, which limits how much the intercept may carry.



Availability

Available on request. The papers are unpublished, so source code and wheels are not posted publicly. Academic users may request them at yang.liu19@imperial.ac.uk, stating name, institution and intended use. They receive the frozen v1.2.0 release: the naipca and gcde wheels with SHA-256 sidecars, the certification package (release and configuration-freeze certificates, parity and warm-start test logs, release hashes), runnable examples that need no proprietary data, and the research estimation drivers with a one-window audit sample; the licensed characteristics panel is not included. Hiring teams may instead ask by email (subject “NA-IPCA walkthrough”) for a short walkthrough of the code, its test logs and an audit record. Please cite: Liu, M. (2026). NA-IPCA: Geometry-Aware Characteristic-Based Asset Pricing (QZ-IPCA and NA-IPCA toolkits), version 1.2.0.



Handbook and licence
The NA-IPCA Handbook (Draft 4.1, July 2026, 189 pages; not in the release) covers notation, ruler construction and selection, the estimation algorithm, options, diagnostics, debugging and a practitioner’s decision flow. Licence: NA-IPCA Academic Research License v1.0 (July 2026): free for academic research, teaching, replication and benchmarking with citation; commercial use, redistribution and derivative toolkits need written permission; modified copies must not pose as the certified release.

title: Macro Forecast Evaluation & Regime Diagnostics
text:
What it helps answer
Questions a researcher or portfolio manager can put to any forecasting comparison with this workflow:

Did the new predictor reduce errors on the same origins, or only on a different sample?
Is the difference larger than sampling error, once the overlap of multi-step forecasts is allowed for?
Does the conclusion survive a change of sample start, output version or training rule?
Were the losses accumulated steadily or in one episode?
Which inputs would not have been known at the forecast origin?

title: Macro Forecast Evaluation & Regime Diagnostics
text:
Inputs









Input
In the UK example
Requirement for a new application




Target and horizon
Change in the services CPI 12-month rate (ONS series D7NN) over 3 and 6 months, in percentage points
One definition shared by every model


Forecast origins
Origin month t, with data for month t treated as known (in practice CPI for t is published in month t + 1 and labour-market data later). M1–M4 and M6 from 2006 (latest run) or 2010 (research-summary run); M0 from 2001 or 2005; M5 from 2016 or 2020; up to the last month with an observed outcome (September 2025 at 3 months, June 2025 at 6 months)
The same origins for every model in a comparison


Predictors
Services inflation, private-sector regular pay growth, a labour-market slack index, and three representations of persistence
A timestamp saying when each value was first available


Model forecasts
Per-origin records: origin, horizon, model, outcome, forecast
One record per model, origin and horizon


Baseline
M2, a Phillips-style model with a fixed specification (coefficients re-estimated at every origin)
Fixed before the comparison is run

title: Macro Forecast Evaluation & Regime Diagnostics
text:
Analyses

Ingest Read the per-origin forecast records of each archived run and the persistence series. Implemented & tested.
Validate Check that every model has the expected forecasts, that outcomes agree across models at each origin, that errors equal outcome minus forecast, and that months are consecutive. Implemented & tested (unit tests feed synthetic invalid records to each check).
Configure Choose the output version, horizon, model and comparison window with the controls below. Implemented (the controls select among precomputed results; every combination is tested in the JSON).
Compute RMSE, MAE, direction hit rate and n; RMSE relative to M2; the loss differential, its running sum, and a Diebold–Mariano test with the original equal-weight long-run variance and the Harvey–Leybourne–Newbold correction, with a Newey–West (Bartlett) variance as a sensitivity. Implemented & tested (unit tests on synthetic cases and a pinned reference value; parity with the archived model-comparison tables to 10⁻⁹).
Compare Own windows against the common window, three output versions side by side, and errors split by the signal state. Implemented & tested.
Interpret and export Charts with numeric tables, a static table of the default view, and the full computed data as JSON. Implemented & tested.

title: Macro Forecast Evaluation & Regime Diagnostics
text:
Interactive demonstration

The interactive view needs JavaScript. The image shows the default view (latest run, 3 months, M4 against M2, common window); the static table under Outputs carries its numbers.
The controls switch among results computed at build time from the archived records: every combination is a distinct calculation, not a relabelling. The default view is the latest archived run, 3 months, M4 against M2, common window. The third output version re-estimates the latest run with training restricted to outcomes observed by the origin; it removes only the overlapping training targets, and the smoothed state, full-sample z-scores and latest-vintage data still carry look-ahead.



Step 1: Measure persistence


Figure 1: How persistent is UK services inflation? Two estimates that answer different questions, with services and goods CPI below.

Interactive figure: it needs JavaScript. The static image at the start of this section shows both persistence estimates; the monthly values are in forecast_eval.json.



How to read it. Persistence is the autoregressive coefficient of 3-month annualised services inflation. The rolling estimate (dashed) uses only the previous 120 months at each date, so it uses no later months (apart from publication lags and the latest data vintage). The smoothed state-space estimate (solid, with its 68% band) uses the whole sample, including later months: it is a retrospective description, not information available at a forecast origin. The grey span marks months when the smoothed estimate stayed below the threshold for three consecutive months (the durable low-persistence signal); there is one such episode, September 2013 to February 2018. Estimates come from the latest archived run (sample from 2001); the controls do not change this figure. Source: ONS MM23 release of 18 February 2026 (Open Government Licence), series D7NN and D7NM; persistence estimates from the author’s archived research outputs, 24 February 2026.




Step 2: Design a fair comparison


Origin The same forecast origin t for every model
Target Each model forecasts y(t, h): services inflation at t + h minus at t
Error Outcome minus forecast, once the outcome is observed
Score RMSE and the loss differential on the origins all models share


Each model is re-estimated at every origin by least squares on an expanding window (at least 60 months), one regression per horizon (direct multi-step forecasts). The persistence models need extra history: in the latest run M5’s rolling estimate starts in December 2010 (in the research-summary run, later), so M5 has the fewest origins. Scoring each model on its own window therefore compares different periods; the common window removes that difference but is set by the shortest model.


Figure 2: Which origins does each model cover? Own windows (bars) and the common window (shaded), for the chosen version and horizon.

Interactive figure: it needs JavaScript. The default view's numbers are in the static tables under Outputs.


How to read it. Each bar runs from a model’s first to its last forecast origin with an observed outcome; n is the number of origins. The highlighted bar is the model chosen above; M2, the baseline, is dark grey. The shaded band is the common window used when “Common window” is selected. Source: computed at build time from the per-origin records of the author’s archived research outputs (February 2026 release of the study).




Step 3: Inspect errors


Table 1: Forecast errors by model. RMSE, MAE, direction hit rate and n for the chosen version, horizon and window.

Interactive figure: it needs JavaScript. The default view's numbers are in the static tables under Outputs.


How to read it. Errors are in percentage points of the 12-month rate. RMSE vs M2 = 100 × (model RMSE ÷ M2 RMSE − 1): negative means smaller errors than M2, positive means larger. Direction hit rate is the share of origins where the forecast change has the same sign as the outcome (the no-change model M0 forecasts zero and scores low by construction). On own windows, the main ratio uses the origins each model shares with M2; the archived-table column divides by M2’s RMSE on M2’s own origins, so it mixes periods (for M5 it even changes sign). Source: computed at build time from the author’s archived research outputs (February 2026 release of the study); matches the archived model-comparison tables to 10⁻⁹.




Step 4: Test robustness


Figure 3: Is the difference larger than sampling error, and when did it build up? Cumulative loss differential, the Diebold–Mariano test, and the same comparison across versions and windows.

Interactive figure: it needs JavaScript. The default view's numbers are in the static tables under Outputs.





How to read it. The loss differential at each origin is d = (model error)² − (M2 error)². The line is its running sum: it rises when the model’s error is larger than M2’s. The Diebold–Mariano statistic divides the mean of d by a long-run standard error with h − 1 lags, because forecasts h months ahead overlap (their errors are serially correlated up to lag h − 1); as in the original test, the first h − 1 autocovariances get equal weights (a rectangular kernel). The Harvey–Leybourne–Newbold correction adjusts it for short samples, and the p-value is two-sided from a t distribution. The p-value depends on the variance estimator: with Newey–West (Bartlett) weights, also shown, the smallest p-value on the page (M6, 6 months, observed-outcomes version, common window) falls from 0.07 to 0.02. For nested pairs (M0 and M1 inside M2, M2 inside M6) the DM statistic has a non-standard limiting distribution under recursive estimation, so the t reference distribution does not apply; a Clark–West adjustment would be the appropriate test, so those p-values are indicative only. Under the null of equal population accuracy, the larger model of a nested pair is expected to show slightly larger errors in a finite sample, because it estimates extra coefficients. Failing to reject equal accuracy is not evidence that two models are equally accurate: with a sample of this size and overlapping errors, the test has low power. The signal-state split uses the signal that enters M4 (previous month); the signal is derived from the smoothed estimate, a retrospective classification not known at the forecast origin, and there is only one signal episode, so the split is close to a split by period. Source: computed at build time from the author’s archived research outputs (February 2026 release of the study).



What this shows. The answer depends on the version and on the evaluation window. On the common window, M4’s RMSE is 0.68% (3 months) and 3.09% (6 months) lower than M2’s in the research-summary run (sample from 2005, origins from January 2020), but 2.99% and 3.40% higher in the latest run (sample from 2001, origins from January 2016). Much of that difference comes from the evaluation window: scored on the research-summary run’s window (from January 2020), the latest run gives +0.51% at 3 months and −4.04% at 6 months. The remaining change (sample start 2001 rather than 2005, added earnings and vacancies inputs) cannot be separated in the archive. The re-estimation that trains only on observed outcomes keeps the sign of the latest run (+2.82% and +1.64%, against +2.99% and +3.40%; its common windows start h − 1 months later, in March and June 2016); it does not remove the other look-ahead listed under Limitations. In the latest run, the cumulative loss differential builds up from 2018 to 2020, after the only signal episode ended in February 2018, and partly reverses in 2021–2022; a few years, not a steady pattern, drive the gap. No p-value from the main test (equal-weight variance with the HLN correction) is below 0.05. The smallest, 0.07, is for M6, which is worse than M2 in the observed-outcomes version at 6 months (+6.81%); with the Bartlett variance it is 0.02, and among 80 tests with no multiple-testing adjustment one such result is to be expected. A model ranking from one window or one version is not robust here.
