title: Macro Forecast Evaluation & Regime Diagnostics
text:
How to use and adapt
Other variables, predictors, models or countries need matched, properly licensed data, re-estimation at every origin and a fresh pseudo-out-of-sample evaluation on matched windows. The archived exercise is not an always-current inflation forecast and is not connected to live data feeds.

Step 5: Adapt to other variables, predictors or countries
The evaluation functions (errors, relative RMSE, Diebold–Mariano, cumulative loss) take a table of per-origin records (origin, horizon, model, outcome, forecast) and are tested on synthetic data and on the two UK runs; a loader for new record files is a Planned extension. Producing those records for a new question takes upstream work that this page does not do:

Define the target and its timing. Choose the series and horizons, and record when each value is published; use historical vintages where they exist.
Build predictors that were available at the origin. Lag each predictor by its publication delay, and use filtered or rolling estimates rather than smoothed ones.
Re-estimate every model at every origin, training only on outcomes already observed at that origin, and write the per-origin records.
Evaluate on matched origins with the same baseline, horizon and target, then run the version and window checks above.

What is tested: the evaluation computations (unit tests, parity with the archived tables), the input checks (synthetic invalid records) and the expanding-window forecasting function, which reproduces the latest UK run’s stored forecasts to 10⁻¹⁰. What is not: data download, the state-space estimation, and any other variable, predictor or country (Planned extension). The UK results are not results for new inputs; a new predictor needs its own data-timing checks, re-estimation and a matched pseudo-out-of-sample window.

title: Macro Forecast Evaluation & Regime Diagnostics
text:
Historical example, evidence and limitations
UK services inflation, archived research example (February 2026). A short research study of whether changes in the persistence of UK services inflation help to forecast it, written in February 2026 as a research snapshot.








Model
Predictors (values for the origin month unless marked)




M0 No change
Forecast change set to zero


M1 AR(1)-style
Services inflation


M2 Fixed-specification Phillips-style baseline
Services inflation, wage growth, labour-market slack


M3 Slack replaced by smoothed persistence
Services inflation, wage growth, smoothed persistence (previous month)


M4 Slack replaced by durable signal
Services inflation, wage growth, durable low-persistence signal from the smoothed estimate (previous month)


M5 Slack replaced by rolling persistence
Services inflation, wage growth, rolling 120-month persistence (previous month)


M6 Regime-gated Phillips (M4v2; latest run only)
M2’s predictors, the signal (previous month), and the signal times inflation and wage growth




M3–M5 drop the slack index, so their comparison with M2 swaps one predictor for another; M6 is the only model that adds the signal to M2’s predictors.

Sources. Office for National Statistics: consumer price inflation (MM23; services D7NN, goods D7NM), labour market statistics, average weekly earnings (private-sector regular pay), vacancies; Open Government Licence v3.0. Bank of England: nominal gilt yield curves, used in the original study’s rates cross-check only; they do not enter the forecasts evaluated here.
Output versions. The run of 23 February 2026 (sample from 2005, models M0–M5) is the version behind the author’s February 2026 research summary.1 The run of 24 February 2026 (sample from 2001, models M0–M6) is the latest. The common windows differ (from January 2020 and from January 2016), because M5 starts later in the shorter sample. Scoring the latest run on the earlier window isolates that part: on the research-summary run’s window the latest run gives +0.51% (3 months, n = 69, p = 0.91) and −4.04% (6 months, n = 66, p = 0.61) for M4 against M2. The later run also moved the sample start and added the earnings and vacancies files to its inputs; the archive cannot separate those two changes. The third version is computed here and is not archived: the latest run’s inputs, with training restricted to outcomes observed by the origin.
Reproduction scope. Evaluation computations: recomputed from the per-origin records of both runs and tested (Implemented & tested). Forecasts of the latest run: re-estimated from its archived processed inputs, matching the stored forecasts to 10⁻¹⁰. Data download, the state-space smoother and the rolling regressions were not rerun (Archived research example). The research-summary run’s processed inputs were overwritten by the later run, so its forecasts are evaluated as archived and cannot be split by signal state. The parity results and SHA-256 hashes of the archived source files are recorded in the meta block of forecast_eval.json.
Limitations. The design is pseudo-out-of-sample (recursive re-estimation, forecasts scored only after the origin), but not strictly so: a strict test uses only data available at the origin, and these forecasts also use later information (items 1 to 4; only the use of the latest data vintage in item 3 is the usual pseudo-out-of-sample simplification). (1) M3, M4 and M6 use the smoothed persistence estimate, which draws on later data; lagging it one month does not make it available at the origin. The signal threshold is also set from the 2001–2019 distribution of the smoothed estimate, so for earlier origins it uses later information. Only M5’s rolling estimate is backward-looking. (2) The archived training rule includes the last h − 1 outcomes, which are observed only after the origin; the observed-outcomes version removes only these, and the smoothed state, full-sample z-scores and latest-vintage data still carry look-ahead. (3) Values are dated by reference month, not release date, from the latest vintage: CPI for a month is published in the following month, labour-market data later and subject to revision. (4) The slack index combines z-scores computed over the full sample. (5) Common windows are short (66 to 117 origins), errors overlap, and no adjustment is made for testing several models, horizons and versions: the controls give access to 80 p-values, and at the 5% level a few would fall below 0.05 by chance alone. (6) One signal episode only. (7) M0 and M1 are nested in M2, and M2 in M6, so the DM p-values of M0, M1 and M6 against M2 are indicative only.

Dated note on the research-summary figures. The author’s February 2026 research summary reported that, on the common window, M4’s RMSE was 0.68% lower than M2’s at 3 months and 3.09% lower at 6 months. Research tools
Each tool below is a reusable analysis function, demonstrated on one archived research example. The example data are historical; each page shows the function: its inputs, its outputs and where it stops. The Research Toolkit menu collects them, with an overview.


Implemented & tested: diagnostic code · portfolio risk diagnostics · example: Archived research example

Return-State Behavior Profile
Portfolio behaviour and risk diagnostics
How did a return stream behave in normal months, strong rallies, recoveries, downturns and tail months? From dated strategy and benchmark returns, the function computes conditional returns, downside beta and hit frequencies for each market state, with observation counts and small-sample warnings.


Example data: an archived systematic long–short U.S. equity strategy backtest, monthly data Apr 2007 – Nov 2025 (224 months); a research case study, not an audited track record, and a configuration selected from several in an earlier study (selection bias not corrected); its signal loadings were estimated on a sample that may overlap the backtest period, so it is not an out-of-sample result.
Interactive demonstration: 7 return streams (four archived, three built from public market and Treasury-bill returns) × 3 state definitions on the full sample, 21 results computed at build time. Half-sample results are not published, because they would let single months of the private stream be reconstructed.
Not claimed: future returns, actual trading, or a factor swap on fixed data; a new factor needs a new backtest before these diagnostics apply.

Macro Forecast Evaluation & Regime Diagnostics
Forecast evaluation workbench
How should competing forecasts be judged when economic relationships change? From per-origin forecast records, the function scores models on the same origins, horizon and target, tracks the cumulative loss differential and tests the null of equal predictive accuracy (Diebold–Mariano test), next to a monitor of inflation persistence.


Example data: UK services inflation, February 2026 research snapshot; ONS monthly data through Dec 2025.
Interactive demonstration: output version, horizon, model and comparison window switch among results computed at build time from the archived records.
Not claimed: a forecast, an operational forecasting service, or that one model forecasts better in general.

Terms used on these pages. To say how much of a stock’s expected return each driver explains, a model must first decide when two combinations of characteristics are really different, and how large each one is; the rule it uses is the ruler (formally, a metric: an inner product on combinations of characteristics). A combination (a direction) gives every stock a score; it is not a portfolio. The plain ruler (the Euclidean or identity metric) judges a direction by its weights alone; the characteristic ruler (the Gram metric, taken from the characteristics’ cross-sectional Gram matrix) judges it by the scores it gives real stocks. A ruler is a measurement convention, not a better model. IPCA (instrumented principal component analysis) is a latent-factor model whose loadings are linear in stock characteristics; NA-IPCA (No-Arbitrage IPCA) rebuilds it on the characteristic ruler and adds a capped intercept, the part of expected return no factor in the model explains.

title: Projects
text:
Machine learning and portfolios
Factor-model forecasts, rolling U.S. backtests and controlled comparisons, followed to holdings, risk and costs.


Measured · working paper, October 2026

Which positions a factor model represents: exposures, hedges and holdings
Expanding an IPCA library from 36 to 153 U.S. stock characteristics raises in-sample fit, yet the model’s factors represent momentum and size positions less fully. Measured on the stocks actually held, a hedge built with the plain ruler leaves 46.10% of a value position, by squared stock weight, still lined up with the model’s factor loadings (pp. 4–6). A check to run before trusting a better-fitting model for hedging.


225 monthly formation dates, March 2007 to November 2025; models re-estimated each March on the previous 240 months, 19 times (Section II.A, p. 9; Table I, p. 10).
Three latent factors plus six observed ones (market, size, value, profitability, investment and momentum), with and without a characteristic intercept, on 36 and 153 Jensen–Kelly–Pedersen characteristics in 11 economic groups (Section II.B, p. 11; Table I, p. 10).
Stocks split permanently into disjoint source and target groups by a fixed hash: the factors are learned on one group and evaluated on the other (p. 9).
Hedging rules compared at the same characteristic target: the plain-ruler (coefficient) hedge, the loading-neutral hedge measured on current stocks, and a historical minimum-variance hedge (Section V, pp. 24–25).
Gross holdings, one-way turnover and subsequent variance for every policy, with simultaneous intervals over families of twelve comparisons from a twelve-month block bootstrap (Section II.C, pp. 12–15); turnover measures trading volume, not costs (p. 13).

title: NA-IPCA toolkit: estimation code with an audit trail
text:
What the packages are for
To say how much of a stock’s expected return each driver explains, a model must first decide when two combinations of characteristics are really different, and how large each one is. The rule it uses for that is the ruler: formally, a metric (an inner product) on combinations of characteristics. IPCA (instrumented principal component analysis) is a latent-factor model whose loadings are linear in stock characteristics and which measures with the plain ruler (the Euclidean or identity metric); QZ-IPCA measures the same model with the characteristic ruler (the Gram metric); NA-IPCA adds a capped intercept, the part of expected return that no factor in the model explains. The theory is in Geometric Framework and Characteristic-Space Metrics; these packages implement it.

How it is called
from naipca import fit_naipca, load_frozen_config, diagnostics_summary

# D: data mapping; Q: characteristic geometry from the GCDE toolkit
config = load_frozen_config(overrides={"max_outer": 1000, "tol_outer": 1e-6})
result = fit_naipca(D, geometry={"Q": Q, "method": "raw_mean_w"},
                    K_lat=3, K_obs=5, delta=0.05, opts=config.options)
print(diagnostics_summary(result))

The quick-start sketch from the toolkit’s README. K_lat, K_obs: numbers of latent and observed factors; delta: the cap on how much the intercept may carry.

title: Return-State Behavior Profile
text:
What it helps answer
The profile goes beyond a single average or ratio: it shows when a return stream earned what it earned, and how much evidence stands behind each number. Questions it helps a portfolio manager or researcher ask:

Is risk exposure asymmetric? Compare downside beta (with its interval) and downside returns with the mean return in normal months (Carry) and with the all-months row.
Do apparent tail characteristics rest on too few observations? The tail state holds 12 months; the stream was positive in 9 of them (75%), and the 95% confidence interval for that share runs from 42.8% to 94.5%.
Does the record lean on recoveries, normal-month returns or rare extremes? Read the five return metrics side by side, with n.
How fragile is the diagnosis to the state definition? Switch to quintiles or a deeper recovery threshold, and watch which spokes move.
How much of a sleeve’s change comes from the strategy, and how much from holding less equity? Compare Proxy + 5% strategy with Proxy + 5% cash (reference) (and the 10% pair): the sleeve is funded pro rata, so equity falls to 57% or 54% either way. These are descriptive blends, not allocation recommendations.

It does not forecast returns, estimate capacity or establish that a strategy will behave the same way next time.

How to read it. In the radar, each spoke is one metric on a custom scale from 0 (centre) to 1 (rim); the solid outline is the selected stream and the dashed outline the benchmark. The scale is a display device, not a probability or a rating: return metrics map −5% a month to 0 and +5% to 1, downside beta is inverted (the benchmark’s own beta of 1 scores 0.25), and values beyond the range are clipped. A larger radius is not uniformly “better”; read the raw values in the table. Hollow squares mark clipped scores. On the downside and tail spokes (4–8) the benchmark’s values are set by the state definition (its beta is 1 and its returns are at or below the cut-off), so the grey diamonds mark the cut-off, not a performance comparison. In the default view, spokes 4–8 are all computed on the same 23 downside months (the 12 tail months are among them), so five of the eight spokes, and most of the polygon’s shape, rest on 23 of the 224 months. The table gives a 95% confidence interval for each of the stream’s values; the intervals treat months as independent and are descriptive, and a wide interval means the history cannot pin the value down. Raw values switches the chart to the metrics in their own units. Reliability is the share of a state’s months with a positive return: a historical hit rate, not a probability. Source: the author’s archived white paper (2026; titled “Regime-Aware Alpha Strategy”), monthly backtest tables; diagnostics computed by this site’s pipeline. Data

Method notes. States are set by the benchmark, never by the stream being diagnosed. Percentiles are estimated on all months of the selected window, so the classification is retrospective, not an ex-ante trading signal. The recovery rule reads the benchmark drawdown from April 2007 onwards, so the first month of a window can qualify. States overlap: tail months are also downside months, and many strong-rally months are also recovery months. Upside Participation is called Positive Convexity in the white paper; it is a conditional mean, not an estimate of convexity in the mathematical sense. Likewise, Carry is the mean return in normal months, not carry in the usual sense of the return earned if prices do not change. The benchmark defines the states, so its downside beta (1), downside and tail means (below the cut-off) and hit rates (0) are fixed or bounded by construction. The normalisation is the author’s own display scale for putting eight metrics on one chart; a score of 0 or 1 often reflects clipping, not significance, and clipped scores are flagged. Intervals: t-intervals for means and betas (OLS standard error), Clopper–Pearson (exact binomial) intervals for hit rates, all treating months as independent; overlapping states and the selection of the configuration are not accounted for. The tool keeps the specification’s product name, Return-State Behavior Profile, in US spelling; the text uses British spelling.
Output contract. Each result carries metric name, raw value, units, standard error and 95% interval, normalised score with a clipping flag, a flag where the benchmark’s value is set by the state definition, state rule, n, date range, benchmark, normalisation formula, data provenance and warnings, plus an all-months reference row; the CSV export above writes exactly these fields for the current view. Dates. The data period (monthly backtest data, Apr 2007 – Nov 2025) is fixed by the archive; the build date shown above the chart is only when the site recomputed the diagnostics from it.

title: Return-State Behavior Profile
text:
How to use and adapt
The diagnostics are the last layer of a longer chain. Changing the stream is a matter for this page; changing the factor or signal behind a stream is not.

Another strategy. Supply a rights-cleared monthly return stream and its benchmark in the input format above, then recompute the diagnostics. Validating the loader on a stream other than this archive is a planned extension.
Another alpha factor or signal. First rebuild the signals and the portfolio and backtest them. A factor name cannot be swapped into this return-level analysis: the analyser sees only the returns that the upstream chain produces.
Whether the model adds anything. That the NA-IPCA signal does better than simpler characteristic signals is a hypothesis this page does not test. A test would need a second upstream backtest under the same portfolio rule and costs (for example, a plain IPCA or single-characteristic signal), with all loadings estimated only on data before the test period, and the two return streams compared on the same months, state by state, with these diagnostics.



Layer 1 · upstream Factor or model inputs Planned extension
Layer 1 · upstream Point-in-time signal
Layer 1 · upstream Portfolio weights, costs, rebalancing
Layer 1 → 2 · interface Monthly return stream (+ benchmark)
Layer 2 · this page runs here Return-State diagnostics Implemented & tested


Dashed boxes are upstream research that this page does not run. A new factor or signal changes Layer 1, so it needs a new backtest (signal, weights, costs) before its return stream exists; only then do the same diagnostics apply. A factor drop-down on fixed return data would only relabel the same numbers, so none is offered.
The real upstream chain of this example (documentation only; not rerun here):


153 stock characteristics (the JKP library), rank-normalised each month.
NA-IPCA alpha loadings, estimated in an earlier study by the author: one fixed set, applied unchanged to every formation month (Mar 2007 – Oct 2025). Its estimation sample is not documented here and may overlap the backtest period.
Signal: each stock’s score is its characteristics times those loadings, s = z′Γα.
Portfolio: rank all stocks in the universe each formation month; long the top 5%, short the bottom 5%, equal weights (about +1 long and −1 short).
Quarterly rebalancing with a three-month holding period.
Gross monthly return, minus a bid-ask cost proxy on rebalancing months (each stock’s estimated one-way bid-ask cost times the change in its weight): the net stream diagnosed here.


Selection caveat. This configuration was the best among several variants (stock universe, tail fraction, holding period) compared in an earlier strategy-screening study by the author. Its backtest therefore carries selection bias, and the diagnostics describe the selected stream without correcting for that search. Because the loadings are one fixed set whose estimation sample may overlap the backtest, the stream should not be read as an out-of-sample result either.

title: Return-State Behavior Profile
text:
Historical example, evidence and limitations

Archived research example

What. A long–short U.S. equity backtest built on NA-IPCA characteristic signals, from the author’s archived white paper (2026; titled “Regime-Aware Alpha Strategy”, although the portfolio rule has no regime switch): monthly returns, Apr 2007 – Nov 2025, 224 months, net of a bid-ask cost proxy, with the gross stream and a 60% U.S. equity + 40% cash proxy alongside.
Status. Historical backtest. Not actual trading, not audited, not independently replicated from the raw inputs. The cost proxy charges each stock’s estimated one-way bid-ask cost on the change in its weight at rebalancing (about one month in three); it lowers the mean return by 0.73 percentage points a month over all 224 months, and the normal-month mean from 1.91% (gross) to 1.26% (net), so the results are sensitive to this assumption. Borrow and financing costs and market impact are not modelled; the portfolio is equal-weighted across the whole stock universe, and capacity is not tested. The configuration was selected in an earlier study, and the estimation sample of its signal loadings may overlap the backtest period (see the caveats above).
Reproduction scope. The site pipeline (pipeline/exhibits/return_state.py) recomputes all eight metrics from the archived monthly records and matches the stored radar table to within 1 × 10⁻⁸ (largest difference about 2 × 10⁻¹⁵); the author’s separate recompute script also passes on the same file. Both are internal consistency checks of the supplied data, not an audit of the backtest or its inputs.
Public factor returns. The archive also carries Fama–French long–short factor returns (from the Kenneth R. French Data Library: gross, no costs). Compared with the library’s monthly files retrieved on 11 October 2026 (F-F_Research_Data_5_Factors_2x3 and F-F_Momentum_Factor, built from the August 2026 CRSP database), those columns differ in some months; the largest difference for each factor ranges from 0.2 to 1.7 percentage points, most likely reflecting later revisions of the library, so they are not offered as streams here. The market and risk-free columns match the library exactly.
Limitations. Retrospective, overlapping states; 12 tail months; intervals that treat months as independent and ignore the selection of the configuration; a custom display scale with clipping; one benchmark choice; one archived strategy. Stability over time: half-sample results are not published, because they would let single months of the private stream be reconstructed; an internal check found that the downside profile differs markedly between the first and second halves of the sample, so the full-sample profile should not be read as a stable trait.
Data rights. The monthly return streams are not published. This page and its JSON carry aggregates only: per-state counts, thresholds, the eight metrics with their intervals and an all-months reference row. Before publication the pipeline runs a disclosure screen: it treats each published mean and beta numerator as a linear equation in the private monthly returns, and each sum of squares implied by the intervals as a linear equation in their squares, and it refuses to publish if any month’s leverage in either system (its diagonal entry in the projection matrix onto the space the equations span) reaches 0.75, a limit the author set (largest value here 0.70; a value of 1 would mean that a month can be solved exactly). The screen rules out exact recovery of a single month from these linear equations and the public market returns. It does not model the counts of positive months, nonlinear combinations of the statistics, outside information or approximate inference about a month, so it is a heuristic safeguard, not a privacy guarantee. Benchmark and cash returns come from the Kenneth R. French Data Library (Mkt-RF plus RF, built from CRSP) and are cited as such; this page publishes only aggregates computed from them, not the library’s files.

title: Quantitative Research Toolkit
text:
These tools show how I turn financial data into diagnostics that can be checked, for investment research and model review. Each tool page states what the tool reads, computes and returns, and where it stops, and runs it on one historical research example. The examples show how a tool works; they do not show that any strategy or model performs better than another, and nothing here is a trading or forecasting service.

title: Quantitative Research Toolkit
text:
Portfolio Risk Diagnostics
Tool page: Return-State Behavior Profile
What it helps answer. How has a return stream behaved in normal months, strong rallies, recoveries, downturns and tail months, and how many months stand behind each figure?








Item
Details




You supply
Dated monthly strategy and benchmark returns for the same months (cash optional). Only the benchmark defines the market states; no factor, signal or stock characteristic enters.


It computes
Market states from the benchmark; conditional mean returns, downside beta and hit rates (share of months with a positive return) in each state, with 95% confidence intervals and observation counts.


It returns
A radar chart with a raw-value table, state rules, observation counts, small-sample warnings and a CSV of the aggregates.


Status
Implemented & tested: diagnostics on seven return streams and three state definitions, full sample. Planned extension: other strategies through the same function, and a new factor, which needs a new upstream backtest first.


Historical example
An archived long–short U.S. equity backtest, monthly data Apr 2007 – Nov 2025 (224 months): not actual trading, not audited, selected from several configurations in an earlier study, and built on signal loadings whose estimation sample may overlap the backtest, so not an out-of-sample result. The tail state holds 12 months, so tail figures describe this sample only.




Explore risk diagnostics

title: Quantitative Research Toolkit
text:
Macro Forecast Evaluation
Tool page: Macro Forecast Evaluation & Regime Diagnostics
What it helps answer. Are one forecasting model’s errors really smaller than another’s on the same dates and target, and is the gap larger than chance, that is, statistically significant?








Item
Details




You supply
Per-origin forecast records (origin, horizon, model, outcome, forecast) for one target shared by every model, and a baseline fixed in advance. A new application also needs the date on which each predictor value was first available (the release date of its first data vintage).


It computes
Forecast errors of every model on the same forecast dates (RMSE, MAE, direction hit rate, count); each model’s RMSE relative to the baseline; how the gap builds up over time (the cumulative squared-error difference); a Diebold–Mariano test of equal predictive accuracy, with the Harvey–Leybourne–Newbold small-sample correction; each model’s own window against the window all models share; output versions side by side.


It returns
Error tables with forecast counts and dates, charts with their numbers, and every computed value as JSON.


Status
Implemented & tested: the evaluation computations, recomputed from archived per-origin forecasts, and the expanding-window forecasting function, which reproduces the latest UK run’s stored forecasts to 10⁻¹⁰. Archived research example (not rerun): the data download, the state-space smoother and the rolling regressions. Planned extension: a loader for new forecast-record files, and other variables, predictors and countries.


Historical example
UK services inflation, February 2026 research snapshot; ONS data through Dec 2025. An expanding-window pseudo-out-of-sample design with documented look-ahead (some inputs were not available at the forecast origin); no p-value from the main test is below 0.05, and the model ranking changes with the output version and the evaluation window.

title: A Geometric Framework for Identification in Characteristic-Based Factor Models
text: Paper (PDF) · SSRN · Current theory paper · BibTeX

title: A Geometric Framework for Identification in Characteristic-Based Factor Models
text:
1 The question
In the agenda, this paper asks the first question: which ruler? The next paper, Characteristic-Space Metrics, asks: once the ruler is chosen, what does it decide, and how precisely?
Firm characteristics overlap and differ in dispersion. Which combinations of them are genuinely distinct sources of priced risk, and which are only near-copies or leftovers?

To say how much of a stock’s expected return each driver explains, a model must first decide when two combinations of characteristics are really different, and how large each one is. The rule it uses for that is the ruler. Give each characteristic a weight and add them up: every stock gets a score. Such a weighted combination is called a direction (it is not a portfolio). The plain ruler (the Euclidean or identity metric) judges a direction by its weights alone. The characteristic ruler (the Gram metric) judges it by the scores it gives real stocks: how large they typically are, and whether two directions’ scores line up across stocks, high on the same stocks and low on the same stocks.
The ruler, then, is the convention a model uses to measure how large a direction is and how much two directions overlap. Two value signals that pick out the same cheap stocks count as overlapping under the characteristic ruler but as unrelated under the plain ruler.

Standard methods such as principal component analysis (PCA), IPCA (Kelly et al. 2019) and many machine-learning estimators of the stochastic discount factor use the plain ruler (the identity metric) (Section 1.1, p. 2); in IPCA, characteristics instrument each stock’s loadings (betas) on the common drivers.
The paper’s model has three blocks: latent (hidden) factors inferred from the data, observed factors such as the market, and the intercept. The intercept is the part of expected return that no factor in this model explains (the home page’s “alpha” is a close relative, measured against a stated benchmark model).
The answer in one sentence. Measure combinations with the characteristic ruler (the Gram metric), taken from how characteristics vary and overlap across stocks; in simulations calibrated to U.S. stocks, with the true priced directions placed by design where characteristics vary most, the estimator built on this ruler (NA-IPCA) recovers them and an IPCA benchmark with no intercept block does not.

title: A Geometric Framework for Identification in Characteristic-Based Factor Models
text:
2 Why it matters
The ruler decides what counts as “different”. Under the plain ruler (identity metric), a model can split one priced direction into two factors, let a latent factor duplicate an observed benchmark factor already in the model, or push priced content into the intercept (Section 1.1, pp. 2–3).

Practical. The paper argues that its ruler stops latent factors from merely reproducing benchmark portfolios, giving users such as portfolio managers a sharper line between priced structure, benchmark factor exposure and residual noise (Sections 1.4–1.5, pp. 5–6). This is argued and simulated, not shown on actual traded portfolios.
Statistical. A good fit does not reveal the right structure: in the paper’s metric sweep (Table 1 below), IPCA has a higher in-sample R² than NA-IPCA while missing the true directions (Table 9, p. 42).

title: A Geometric Framework for Identification in Characteristic-Based Factor Models
text:
3 The argument at a glance


Question. Stocks are described by dozens of characteristics, many of them versions of a few traits (Section 6.2, p. 28). → The question
Why. Because of this overlap, the plain ruler (identity metric) that PCA and IPCA use misjudges which combinations are truly different (Section 1.1, p. 2). → Why it matters
Framework. Estimate the characteristic ruler (the Gram metric Q_Z) from the data and state all the model’s restrictions in it, including the identification restrictions that keep the three blocks apart and the cap on how much the intercept may carry. The result is NA-IPCA. → The framework
Mechanism. Directions that are orthogonal (look unrelated) under the plain ruler can overlap under the characteristic ruler, so orthogonalising the blocks under the characteristic ruler stops double counting. → A simple example
Evidence. The U.S. characteristic ruler is strongly uneven. In the headline simulation NA-IPCA recovers the priced directions and an IPCA benchmark with no intercept block misses them, so the comparison does not isolate the ruler. IPCA comes close to the true directions (0.01–0.06) in the stress-test designs (Tables 17–19). It stays far off (0.73–0.99) in the metric sweep (Table 1 below) and in the correlation sweep, which moves characteristics from unrelated toward the U.S. pattern (Table 10, p. 43). → Design and main results
Contribution. The ruler becomes an explicit, estimated part of the model’s economics. → How it relates to prior work
Boundary. The paper does not test NA-IPCA on real returns or portfolios; a real-data application is left to a separate study (pp. 50–51). → Scope

title: A Geometric Framework for Identification in Characteristic-Based Factor Models
text:
4 The framework
Let Z_t hold L characteristics for the N_t stocks observed in month t. The characteristic ruler (Gram metric) is the long-run average of the characteristics’ cross-sectional second-moment matrix: how they vary and move together across stocks (Section 2, p. 6):

Q_Z = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} \frac{1}{N_t} Z_t^{\top} Z_t .

Under this ruler, the size (norm) of a direction with weights a is (a^{\top} Q_Z a)^{1/2}: roughly, how widely the scores it gives stocks vary. The plain ruler replaces Q_Z with the identity matrix.
Conditional expected excess returns are split into the three blocks (Section 2, p. 7):

\mathbb{E}_t\!\left[r_{t+1}\right] = Z_t\left(\Gamma_\beta f_t + \Gamma_\delta F^{\text{obs}}_t + \Gamma_\alpha\right).

\Gamma_\beta holds the loadings on the latent factors f_t, \Gamma_\delta the loadings on observed factors such as traded benchmarks, and \Gamma_\alpha is the intercept, built from characteristics (Table 1, p. 7). The estimator, No-Arbitrage IPCA (NA-IPCA), states the rules for all three blocks in terms of Q_Z and caps how much the intercept may carry. The cap is the “no-arbitrage” in the name: the tighter it is, the closer the model comes to strict no-arbitrage (Section 2, p. 8). With the plain ruler and an intercept cap so loose that it never binds, NA-IPCA reduces to IPCA (p. 22).


For specialists: the restrictions, the estimator and the inference

In Q_Z, the latent loadings are orthonormal, \Gamma_\beta^{\top} Q_Z \Gamma_\beta = I; the observed and intercept blocks are Q_Z-orthogonal to the latent span; and the intercept’s size is capped, \psi(\Gamma_\alpha) = \Gamma_\alpha^{\top} Q_Z \Gamma_\alpha \le \delta (Section 2, pp. 7–8). NA-IPCA is weighted least squares restricted to this set (Proposition 3.1, p. 14), with rotation-invariant asymptotic inference for the identified spans (Section 4, from p. 17).

title: A Geometric Framework for Identification in Characteristic-Based Factor Models
text:
5 A simple example
Take two characteristics, A and B, say two versions of value, that move together across stocks with correlation ρ. The priced direction uses both equally. Suppose a model puts A in one block and B in another. Under the plain ruler (identity metric) A and B are orthogonal and look unrelated, so each block claims the shared part.

Try this. (1) Set ρ to 0: both splits explain 100% between them. (2) Raise ρ to 0.9: split with the plain ruler, the two blocks claim 190%. What to notice. Split with the characteristic ruler, the total always stays at 100%, because block B is orthogonalised against block A and keeps only what A leaves unexplained. The shared part is counted once.



Figure 1: Two rulers for two correlated characteristics. Illustrative numbers, not the paper’s data.

title: A Geometric Framework for Identification in Characteristic-Based Factor Models
text:
6 Design and main results
The paper estimates the characteristic ruler on the replication panel of Kelly et al. (2019): 37 characteristics including a constant, 12,813 firms, July 1964 to May 2014 (Section 6.1, p. 27; Table 2, p. 28). It then simulates 1,000 stocks over 240 months in 300 Monte Carlo replications, with characteristics drawn to match this ruler. By design, the three latent factors sit where characteristics vary most, the two observed factors are deliberately weak, and the returns contain a nonzero intercept component (Section 7.1, pp. 34–36; Table 7, p. 36). Same simulated data, three estimators: NA-IPCA, an IPCA benchmark with no intercept block, and PCA (Section 7.2, p. 36).


Figure 2: The characteristic ruler is strongly uneven. Share of the total variation (the trace of Q_Z) carried by each of its 15 largest eigenvalues (principal directions).



How to read it. Each bar is one of the 37 directions of Q_Z, largest first. Source: SSRN preprint, March 2026, Figure 2, p. 33 (reproduced from the paper). Paper page



What this shows. One of the 37 columns is a constant (Table 6, p. 32); its diagonal entry of 1 in a trace of 4.01 matches the largest eigenvalue (Table 7, p. 36), so the 25% first bar is essentially that constant. The unevenness is in the rest: if the other 36 were uncorrelated with equal variance, as the plain ruler assumes, each would carry about 2%; the next four carry about 37% between them (Table 5, p. 30). This describes how characteristics overlap, not which directions are priced.



Figure 3: In the headline simulation, NA-IPCA finds the true latent span; IPCA without an intercept block and PCA do not. Subspace distance between the estimated and the true factor directions (the “span”).



How to read it. Left panel (“latent”): latent factors; right panel (“observable”): observed factors. The distance, \lVert \sin\Theta \rVert_F, is 0 for exact recovery and reaches its maximum when the estimated directions are entirely wrong: \sqrt{3} \approx 1.73 for the three latent-factor directions and \sqrt{2} \approx 1.41 for the two observed-factor directions (footnote 10, p. 39). On the observed block the ranking reverses: IPCA 0.23, NA-IPCA 1.40, almost the maximum, so NA-IPCA misses the observed-factor directions. PCA has no observed block, so its right-panel bar is missing, not zero. The paper reads this as the design’s doing: the observed factors were made deliberately weak (Section 7.2, p. 37). Source: SSRN preprint, March 2026, Figure 4, p. 39, and Table 8, p. 38 (reproduced from the paper). Paper page



What this shows. On the scale from 0 to about 1.73, and with the priced directions placed by design where characteristics vary most, NA-IPCA’s latent-factor directions sit 0.011 from the truth. Those of the IPCA benchmark with no intercept block sit 0.73 away, and those of PCA 0.99 away (Table 8, p. 38). On an overlap measure where 0 means fully separated blocks, the IPCA benchmark’s latent and observed blocks overlap by 0.069; NA-IPCA, which keeps them apart by construction, scores 0.0005. The toy’s double counting appears here in a milder form.

section: 7 How it relates to prior work
text:
7 How it relates to prior work
The table lists the closest reference points (Section 1.2, pp. 3–4).









Prior work
What it established
What this paper adds




Approximate factor models (Bai and Ng 2002)
How many common factors a large panel has, under weak dependence
Once the number is set, asks which directions are priced, measured with an estimated ruler


IPCA (Kelly et al. 2019)
Characteristics instrument time-varying betas; the model admits an intercept and observed factors and tests whether each is zero
States the model’s normalisation and block separation in the characteristic ruler (Gram metric) and caps how much the intercept may carry


RP-PCA, risk-premium PCA (Lettau and Pelger 2020)
Adding a pricing-error penalty to PCA gives factors that also fit average returns
Puts pricing discipline into the set of admissible models, through the ruler and the intercept cap


Shrinking the cross-section (Kozak et al. 2020)
A prior that shrinks the stochastic discount factor’s coefficients on characteristic portfolios, most strongly along their low-variance principal components
Uses the characteristic ruler not as a penalty but to set the model’s scale and keep its blocks apart




The simulations’ weak observed factors follow work on weak and spurious factors (Bryzgalova 2015; Kozak et al. 2018) (p. 32); the intercept cap is related to volatility bounds (Hansen and Jagannathan 1991) (p. 10).
Much prior work first extracts factors with a fixed ruler and then adds pricing restrictions on top (Section 1.2, p. 4). This paper makes the ruler itself something to estimate. The tools are known; what is new is an estimator and inference built on that estimated ruler.
This is the earliest paper in the agenda to set out the idea that runs through it: take the ruler from the data, and state the model’s restrictions in it. Characteristic-Space Metrics states the ruler’s role precisely: it decides the split, not the fit, and its estimation error belongs in the standard errors. Interpreting Pricing Errors holds the ruler fixed to read alphas fairly. Same Forecasts, Different Portfolios, which cites this paper for NA-IPCA (footnote 3, p. 10), shows that the ruler’s units can move portfolios while forecasts barely move; The Ruler Matters measures the ruler on the stocks to ask which positions a model’s factors represent and what hedging them requires.

title: A Geometric Framework for Identification in Characteristic-Based Factor Models
text:
8 Scope

The paper does not test NA-IPCA on real returns or portfolios. In its simulations, out-of-sample return R² is the same for both estimators (Table 19, p. 64); a full out-of-sample application in U.S. equities is left to a separate study (Section 8, pp. 50–51).
In the simulations the true priced directions sit, by design, where characteristics vary most, and the IPCA benchmark lacks the intercept block that the simulated returns contain (Sections 7.1–7.2, pp. 34–36). So the comparison does not isolate the ruler, and it cannot tell which ruler real markets follow.
The characteristic ruler (Gram metric Q_Z) is estimated from one sample, 1964 to 2014. If the distribution of characteristics shifts, the ruler should be re-estimated (Section 8, p. 50).
The intercept is a capped part of expected returns that the factors leave unexplained. It is not a measured mispricing.
The large-sample theory holds only under the conditions the paper states. Its efficiency result is local: among estimators that respect the paper’s restrictions, NA-IPCA reaches the efficiency bound (Section 4.3, p. 19). The paper does not claim that NA-IPCA is the best estimator in general.

title: Interpreting Estimated Pricing Errors: Evidence from Characteristic-Based Return Forecasts
text: Paper (PDF) · BibTeX

title: Interpreting Estimated Pricing Errors: Evidence from Characteristic-Based Return Forecasts
text:
1 The question
In the agenda, this paper follows Characteristic-Space Metrics and asks: if the ruler (the metric on characteristic space; see the box below) can move expected return between the factors and the intercept (the part of expected return no factor explains), what does a smaller alpha mean? The next paper, Same Forecasts, Different Portfolios, moves from reading the model to acting on it: can the ruler change the portfolio even when the forecast does not change?
If a new model leaves less expected return unexplained, is that because its factors are better, or because it is explaining a different estimate of expected returns? And does the size of that leftover help anyone choose or improve a return forecast?
A characteristic-based model issues an estimate of every stock’s expected return, its forecast, directly from the stock’s characteristics. Separately, its factors define which return patterns count as explained. The forecast therefore splits into a part the factors can produce and a leftover, the alpha component (Section 2.3, p. 7). The paper fits the same model twice, under two sets of training weights (the weight each stock receives in estimation): once counting every stock equally (the equal-weighted model) and once weighting stocks by market value (the value-weighted model).

The ruler, and why it stays fixed here. To say how much of a stock’s expected return each driver explains, a model must first decide when two combinations of characteristics are really different, and how large each one is. The rule it uses for that is the ruler: formally, a metric (an inner product) on characteristic space. Give each characteristic a weight and add them up: every stock gets a score. Such a weighted combination is called a direction (it is not a portfolio). The plain ruler (the Euclidean or identity metric) judges a direction by its weights alone. The characteristic ruler (the Gram metric) judges it by the scores it gives real stocks: how large they typically are, and whether two directions’ scores line up across stocks. The ruler is the convention a model uses to measure how large a direction is and how much two directions overlap. Two value signals that pick out the same cheap stocks count as overlapping under the characteristic ruler but as unrelated (orthogonal) under the plain ruler.
The ruler also turns each leftover into a size in basis points: its norm under the Gram matrix, a root mean square across stocks. Both alphas here are scored with the same ruler, on the same stocks and with the same scoring weights (the paper’s evaluation weights: how every leftover is measured, with every stock equal or weighted by market value). For the headline crossing, the ruler is the characteristic Gram matrix averaged over the months of the full sample, July 1963–November 2025 (Table 1, p. 13); the annual selection tests use the average of the preceding 60 months instead (Section 3.3, p. 10). Either way it is built from characteristic second moments, not return covariances, so it measures signal size, not portfolio risk (p. 6). The paper holds this ruler fixed, as a fair comparison must: the two models differ in their estimate and their factors, never in the ruler.

title: Interpreting Estimated Pricing Errors: Evidence from Characteristic-Based Return Forecasts
text:
2 Why it matters
A smaller alpha is often offered as evidence that a new model’s factors are better. If the gap instead comes from a different estimate of expected returns, the evidence is about that estimate, not the factors (p. 2). A model builder should therefore ask: smaller relative to which estimate? A team choosing a forecast can test that choice, and how much of the alpha component to keep, on later returns.

title: Interpreting Estimated Pricing Errors: Evidence from Characteristic-Based Return Forecasts
text:
3 The argument at a glance


Split. A smaller alpha can mean better factors or a different estimate. → The framework
Problem. Comparing two models’ own alphas mixes the two reasons. → Why it matters
Design. Cross each model’s estimate with each model’s factors, under one ruler (a fixed Gram metric). → A simple example
Finding 1. Swapping only the factors barely moves the leftover; swapping only the estimate closes the gap. → Table 1
Finding 2. Picking the model with the smaller alpha each year adds little to next year’s accuracy. → Figure 2, Table 2
Finding 3. Turning the alpha component down gives more accurate forecasts than keeping it whole in 20 of 24 test settings (specifications), and than simple averaging in only 8. → Figure 3
Boundary. Find out what changed, then test each use against simple alternatives; the evidence is exploratory, not a test of zero alpha or a trading result. → Scope

title: Interpreting Estimated Pricing Errors: Evidence from Characteristic-Based Return Forecasts
text:
4 The framework
The starting point is the pricing error \alpha_t = \mu_t - \beta_t \lambda_t: expected excess returns \mu_t minus what factor exposures (betas) \beta_t and risk prices \lambda_t account for (equation 1, p. 5). It is measured in percent per month. It is an expected quantity, not the noise in realised returns, and a nonzero value is not by itself proof of mispricing.
The empirical model is a characteristic-based factor model in the style of instrumented principal component analysis (IPCA) (Kelly et al. 2019): characteristics set each stock’s loadings on a few latent factors through a loading matrix B, and its intercept through a separate coefficient vector a (equation 2, p. 5). In symbols, with \hat h the model’s expected-return coefficients:

\begin{aligned}
\hat h &= \underbrace{P_Q(B)\,\hat h}_{p:\ \text{factor part}} + \underbrace{[I - P_Q(B)]\,\hat h}_{r:\ \text{alpha component}},\\
h(\eta) &= p + \eta\, r,\qquad \eta \in [0,1].
\end{aligned}

The second line keeps all of p and a fraction \eta of r (equation 14, p. 21): \eta = 1 is the complete forecast, \eta = 0 the factor part alone.


For specialists: the projection and the ruler

If the factor means are set to absorb everything the factors can reproduce, then r, the part left outside, is exactly the model’s fitted characteristic alpha (equation 6, p. 7). P_Q(B) = B(B'QB)^{-1}B'Q is the projection onto the loading space (the return signals the model’s exposures can generate), orthogonal under the inner product that Q defines. Q, the characteristic Gram matrix with equal-stock or capitalisation weights, makes b'Qb, for b the difference between two coefficient vectors, measure how differently they forecast the stocks studied (equations 3 to 5, p. 6). In the crossing, each pairing gets the factor means best suited to its target (p. 7).

title: Interpreting Estimated Pricing Errors: Evidence from Characteristic-Based Return Forecasts
Interpreting Estimated Pricing Errors: Evidence from Characteristic-Based Return Forecasts
text:
6 Design and main results
The data are the U.S. stock panel associated with the characteristic library of Jensen et al. (2023): 153 characteristics, July 1963 to November 2025 (Section 3.1, p. 8). The target is next month’s excess return, clipped (winsorised) at the monthly 1st and 99th percentiles. Forecasts are issued each March from 2017 to 2025 (nine forecast dates, called origins) for the 105 months from April 2017 to December 2025, always from earlier data (a pseudo-out-of-sample design) (Section 3.2, pp. 9–10). Accuracy is prediction R^2, an out-of-sample R^2 against a zero forecast: how much a forecast cuts squared error compared with always predicting zero (equation 11, p. 11).
1. Why is one alpha smaller?

Table 1: Crossing each model’s expected-return estimate with each model’s factors. Size of the leftover under the full-sample characteristic ruler (its Gram-metric norm, a root mean square across stocks), bp a month; equal-stock scoring; three factors (Table 1, p. 13).

How to read it. Bold cells are each model’s own alpha; the other two show how closely one model’s factors reproduce the other’s estimate. Reading down a column changes only the factors; across a row, only the estimate. If better factors were the reason for the gap between the bold cells, the left column would close most of it; if a different estimate were, the top row would.


What this shows. Same estimate, different factors: the leftover barely moves (117.37 to 116.67 bp). Same factors, different estimate: it falls to 75.02 bp (Table 1, p. 13). A symmetric decomposition of the squared gap gives about 101% to the change of estimate and −1% to the change of factors. The −1% is a small offset: on the value-weighted estimate, the equal-weighted model’s factors leave slightly less (75.02 against 77.27 bp). Under capitalisation-weighted scoring the split is 98% and 2% (p. 13). These shares describe squared signal sizes, not causal effects.

2. Does alpha size help pick a forecast? The rule tested: at each origin, issue the forecast of the model with the smaller historical leftover, then check next year’s accuracy (Section 5.1, p. 17). Judged on each model’s own estimate, the value-weighted model always has the smaller alpha, so the rule picks it every year. A fairer version judges both models’ factors against one common estimate: a ridge regression of returns on characteristics (coefficients shrunk towards zero), fitted to the same history (pp. 10–11). The amount by which the value-weighted model’s leftover is smaller against this estimate is its diagnostic advantage.


Figure 2: Diagnostic advantage and later forecast differences. Nine annual origins, common ridge estimate, preceding-60-month characteristic ruler (Figure 2, p. 18).



How to read it. Right of zero, the diagnostic advantage favours the value-weighted (VW) model; above zero, that model then forecast better. Dots in the top-right or bottom-left quadrants are correct calls; crosses are wrong ones. EW marks equal-stock weights. The 2025 block has nine months. Source: Interpreting Estimated Pricing Errors, working paper, September 2026, Figure 2.



What this shows. Similar diagnostic advantages come before opposite outcomes. Under capitalisation-weighted scoring, the diagnostic favours the value-weighted model by about 2.04 bp at the 2022 origin, yet that model’s prediction R^2 then trails by 1.45 percentage points; at 2023 a similar advantage (1.97 bp) comes before a gain of 1.96 points. Balanced accuracy (the average hit rate across the years won by each model) is 47.5% under equal-stock scoring and 41.7% under capitalisation-weighted scoring, below the 50% of always choosing one model (p. 18).


Table 2: Forecast accuracy of each rule over a common evaluation period. Prediction R^2 in percent (larger is better), 105 months, April 2017 to December 2025 (Table 3, p. 19).

How to read it. Each year the selector issues one of the two factor models’ forecasts; pooled ridge fits one ridge regression of returns on characteristics and bypasses the factor model.


What this shows. In the main specification, choosing by alpha size against the common estimate gives less accurate forecasts than simply averaging the two models under both scoring weights (Table 3, p. 19); across the 12 decision sequences of the wider grid it is more accurate than the average in only 5 (p. 20). Averaging is a demanding benchmark, though not always the most accurate: under capitalisation-weighted scoring the value-weighted model alone (1.0491%) is more accurate. Under squared loss, the average’s loss is below the mean of the two component losses by a quarter of their squared disagreement (equation 13, p. 20). With the ruler (the Gram matrix) averaged over the whole training window instead, the selector picks correctly in 6 of 9 years instead of 4 under equal-stock scoring, yet its prediction R^2 (0.3847%) still trails the average (p. 20).

3. Does turning the alpha component down help? The fraction \eta of one model’s alpha component to keep (the smaller it is, the further that component is shrunk towards zero; the paper calls this residual calibration) is estimated from the previous twelve months of completed forecasts, constrained to lie between 0 and 1, and applied to the next year (Section 6.2, p. 22). Figure 3 compares this rule with four baselines (Baseline menu): keeping the component whole; simple averaging; a principal-component (PC) version, which splits the same estimate along the combinations of characteristics that vary most across stocks (the leading eigenvectors of the characteristic Gram matrix) instead of the model’s factors; and scaling the whole forecast by one estimated fraction.


Figure 3: Turning the alpha component down, against a chosen baseline. Gain in prediction R^2, percentage points, 24 test settings, 93 months (the first forecast year is used only to estimate the fraction) (Table G.1, p. 55).

title: Interpreting Estimated Pricing Errors: Evidence from Characteristic-Based Return Forecasts
section: 7 How it relates to prior work
text:
7 How it relates to prior work









Prior work
What it established
What this paper adds




Kelly et al. (2019)
Characteristics set each stock’s factor loadings; an intercept captures characteristic-linked expected return not due to factor exposure.
Asks what a change in the fitted intercept’s size reflects.


Zhang (2024)
Tests of pricing errors in models “with latent factors and firm characteristics as covariances”.
Not a new test; a matched comparison of fitted objects and their forecast use.


Choi and Yuan (2025)
Estimation and inference for “inside” and “outside” alphas, with debiasing.
A different question: what a reported fall in a fitted alpha reflects; no ranking against these estimators (p. 59).


Kozak et al. (2020)
Shrinking a stochastic discount factor over many characteristic portfolios works well out of sample.
Uses ridge as a benchmark; treats keeping part of the alpha component as a separate shrinkage decision.




The tools (projections, ridge regression and forecast averaging) are known; what is new is one matched design that separates the three questions above on the same stocks, dates and loss. In short: mostly a different estimate; little; sometimes. Unfavourable settings are reported alongside favourable ones.
This paper cites Characteristic-Space Metrics for its representation identities (p. 4) (Liu 2026), holds the ruler (the Gram metric) fixed and asks what a smaller estimated alpha means for return forecasting. It deliberately stops at forecasts; Same Forecasts, Different Portfolios and The Ruler Matters carry the agenda into portfolios.
This paper and Same Forecasts, Different Portfolios both ask what the model’s leftover is worth, but in different settings. This paper shrinks one characteristic-based model’s alpha component (keeps an estimated fraction of it) to make forecasts more accurate under squared-error loss. Same Forecasts, Different Portfolios adds the intercept of NA-IPCA (IPCA rebuilt on the characteristic ruler, with a cap on how much the intercept may carry) to expected returns inside one fitted model and measures a portfolio Sharpe ratio gross of transaction costs. The models, objectives and samples differ, so neither result confirms or contradicts the other.

title: Interpreting Estimated Pricing Errors: Evidence from Characteristic-Based Return Forecasts
text:
8 Scope

Not a pricing-error test. The comparisons do not test whether population alphas are zero (Appendix I.2, p. 60).
Not a trading result. Prediction R^2 on clipped next-month returns is not a portfolio return, and no costs or portfolio constraints are modelled (Appendix I.3, p. 60).
Not independent evidence. Nine annual choices and 24 overlapping test settings are sensitivity summaries, not independent replications or confidence intervals (p. 12; Appendix I.2, p. 59).
Not about all alphas. The object is the alpha component that characteristics generate, not every stock-level pricing error (p. 5).
Exploratory history. The sample informed the design, and source-data checks leave some data-vintage and delisting differences unresolved (p. 10; Appendix I.3, p. 60).

title: The Ruler Matters: Factor Exposures, Attribution, and Portfolio Risk
text: Paper with Internet Appendix (PDF, 133 pp.) · BibTeX

title: The Ruler Matters: Factor Exposures, Attribution, and Portfolio Risk
text:
1 The question
In the agenda, this is the last step. Same Forecasts, Different Portfolios showed that the ruler’s units can move a portfolio while forecasts barely move. This paper measures the ruler directly on the stocks, asks which familiar positions a model’s factor loadings represent, and follows the answer to the stocks, trading and risk needed to keep a value, momentum or size tilt.
Same target, different stocks? If a factor model fits returns well, does it represent the positions a value, momentum or size investor cares about? And when the investor hedges with it, does the ruler that measures exposure change which stocks must be held, how much must be traded and how much risk follows?
A factor model gives every stock a loading on each factor: how strongly the stock moves with it. In instrumented principal component analysis (IPCA), a standard factor model, characteristics decide those loadings (Kelly et al. 2019). All the stock positions the loadings can form together make up the model’s loading space. A manager who wants a value, momentum or size tilt without the model’s factor risk removes the part of the position that lies in that space. The paper asks how much of the tilt goes with it, and what it takes to put the tilt back.

The ruler. To say how much of a stock’s expected return each driver explains, a model must first decide when two combinations of characteristics are really different, and how large each one is. The rule it uses for that is the ruler. Give each characteristic a weight and add them up: every stock gets a score. Such a weighted combination is called a direction (it is not a portfolio). The plain ruler (the Euclidean or identity metric) judges a direction by its weights alone. The characteristic ruler (the Gram metric) judges it by the scores it gives real stocks: how large they typically are, and whether two directions’ scores line up across stocks. The ruler is the convention a model uses to measure how large a direction is and how much two directions overlap. Two value signals that pick out the same cheap stocks, such as book-to-market and earnings-to-price, count as overlapping under the characteristic ruler but as unrelated under the plain ruler.
In this paper the characteristic ruler is measured each month on the stocks available that month: the average product of two directions’ scores across those stocks, the cross-sectional second moment of the characteristics, Q_t (Section I.A, eq. 2, p. 3). The paper calls it the stock-exposure ruler. Two directions whose weights look unrelated can still select the same stocks (p. 3). The ruler does not change how IPCA is estimated, and it is not the covariance of stock returns (p. 3; p. 20).

The short answer. Same model, same stocks, same target, different hedge, because the plain ruler judges the loadings by their weights while the hedge holds stocks. If the ruler did not matter, both hedges would leave 0% of a position on the model’s loadings. In the paper’s data, the plain-ruler hedge of a book-to-market position leaves 46.10% on average, and the characteristic-ruler hedge leaves none (Section V.A, p. 24). Beyond this comparison, the paper has three findings. First, fit and representation can part ways: the larger library fits stock returns better, yet its loadings reproduce less of momentum and size. Second, the same fitted returns can be credited very differently to observed and hidden factors. Third, keeping a tilt while removing the loadings needs different stocks, trading and total position size, depending on the library and on how exposure is measured.

title: The Ruler Matters: Factor Exposures, Attribution, and Portfolio Risk
text:
2 Why it matters
Researchers and investors judge a factor model by its fit, but they use it for other things: to say which positions it represents, to credit returns to factors, and to hedge. Each use depends on how exposure is measured, which fit alone does not settle (Section I.B, p. 5).

Economic. A better-fitting model can represent a familiar position less fully. With a free intercept, widening the library from 36 to 153 characteristics raises the model’s total stock-return R² from 17.01% to 17.70% (Table II, p. 17). Over the portfolio sample, the share of the momentum position that the loadings reproduce falls from 82.27% to 62.33% (Section IV.A, p. 22).
Practical. A manager who removes the model’s loadings and then restores the original tilt pays in position size. For larger-firm size with a free intercept, the restored position averages 3.27 times capital in total positions (long plus short) with 36 characteristics, and 1.92 times with 153 (Section V.B, p. 25).
Statistical. The same fitted returns can be credited very differently. For a larger-firm size position, reallocating the exposure that observed and hidden factors share raises the observed factors’ contribution from 1.38 to 45.53 basis points (bp; 1 bp = 0.01 percentage point) a month. The total stays at 2.16 bp (Section VII.A, p. 36).

title: The Ruler Matters: Factor Exposures, Attribution, and Portfolio Risk
text:
3 The argument at a glance


Fit. A larger library fits stock returns better, but that does not show it represents familiar positions better. → Why it matters
Ruler. Measure a direction by the stocks it selects, not by its weights; two directions with unrelated weights can still overlap across stocks. → The framework
Representation. With 153 characteristics, the loadings reproduce less of momentum and size than with 36. → Figure 2
Attribution. Overlapping stock exposures let the same forecast be credited to observed or hidden factors; the total does not move. → Figure 3
Hedging. With the model fixed, the plain-ruler hedge leaves on average 46.10% of a hedged book-to-market position on the loadings (p. 24); keeping a tilt needs different positions in different libraries. → Figure 4, Table 1
Updating. At the same tilt, the policy that measures exposure on this month’s stocks rather than March’s has lower subsequent variance in all twelve exploratory comparisons; nine of twelve simultaneous intervals exclude zero. → Figure 5
Boundary. Shares of stock positions, not of risk or premia; comparisons of complete policies; no trading-cost ledger. → Scope

title: The Ruler Matters: Factor Exposures, Attribution, and Portfolio Risk
text:
4 The framework
The model. Each stock’s next-month excess return is described by a characteristic intercept, six observed factors and three hidden factors, and characteristics set the stock’s loadings on each (Section II.B, eq. 3, p. 11). The intercept is the part of expected return that no factor in this model explains. The observed factors are the market and the Fama–French size, value, profitability and investment factors plus momentum, together FFC6 (Fama and French 1993, 2015; Carhart 1997). The hidden factors (latent factors) are common drivers the model infers from returns; they are statistical, not named economic shocks (p. 2). Hidden factors can be relabelled or mixed without changing what they explain together, so the object of study is their loading space, not any one numbered factor (p. 2).
Coverage. How much of a familiar position can the loadings reproduce? Take the position’s scores across stocks, measure their squared size with one common ruler, and ask what share of it lies in the loading space: 0% means none, 100% means all of it (eq. 10, p. 21). The paper calls this share coverage. It describes stock positions. It is not explained return variance or a risk premium, and the shares of different characteristics are not slices of one budget (p. 5; p. 22).
Two hedges. To keep a tilt without the model’s factor exposure, a manager removes the part of the position that lies in the loading space. Removed with the plain ruler (the paper’s coefficient orthogonality), the position’s characteristic weights become unrelated to the loadings’ weights. Removed with the characteristic ruler on the current stocks, the stocks actually held carry no exposure to any estimated loading, and nothing is invested net (eq. 11, p. 24). The paper calls the second a loading-neutral hedge. Full loading neutrality is a controlled benchmark, not a recommendation to hedge every statistical factor (p. 2).
Tilt and position size. A hedge can also remove part of the intended tilt (the portfolio’s exposure to the named characteristic). Restoring the original tilt then takes larger positions: the total position size (long plus short, per dollar of capital) is the tilt wanted divided by the tilt each unit of position delivers (Section V.B, pp. 24–25).
Three versions of the ruler. The model’s coefficients are re-estimated each March and held for a year. Within the year, exposure can be measured with the training-average version of the characteristic ruler (its average over the previous 240 months), the annual-origin version (March’s stocks, held until February) or the current version (this month’s stocks) (Section VI, p. 31).


For specialists

With Z_t the characteristic matrix of the n_t stocks at formation, directions a and b have stock profiles Z_t a and Z_t b, and (Z_t a)'(Z_t b)/n_t = a'Q_t b with Q_t = Z_t'Z_t/n_t; a'b = 0 need not imply a'Q_t b = 0 (eq. 2, p. 3). Coverage of direction a by loading matrix L under reference Q is

\mathcal{C}(a, L; Q) = \frac{a'QL(L'QL)^{-1}L'Qa}{a'Qa},

invariant to rotations of the hidden factors (eq. 10, p. 21; p. 3). The loading-neutral hedge, with L = [e_0, C, B] (constant, observed-factor and hidden-factor coefficients), is

\tilde w^{Q}_t = \frac{Z_t}{n_t}\left[a - L(L'Q_t L)^{-1}L'Q_t a\right],

the position closest to Z_t a/n_t with zero net stock investment and zero exposure to every column of Z_t L (eq. 11, p. 24). The total position size needed to restore the original tilt satisfies G_t = \xi^0_t/\eta_t = \ell_t/(1 - C^{\text{cash}}_t): a loading-overlap term and a residual-position-shape term (eq. 12, p. 28). With a free intercept, expanding the library changes mean log position size for larger-firm size by −0.525, with contributions of −1.093 from loading overlap and 0.567 from residual shape (p. 29). The identity accounts for positions along the selected direction; it is not the smallest position size over all feasible portfolios (p. 28). Attribution between observed and hidden factors uses A = (B'\bar QB)^{-1}B'\bar QC, C_Q = C - BA and p^Q_{t+1} = p_{t+1} + A g_{t+1}, which leave the joint model unchanged (eq. 13, p. 36).

title: The Ruler Matters: Factor Exposures, Attribution, and Portfolio Risk
The Ruler Matters: Factor Exposures, Attribution, and Portfolio Risk
text:
6 Design and main results
The library is the Jensen–Kelly–Pedersen set (Jensen et al. 2023) of 153 U.S. stock characteristics in 11 economic groups, compared with a fixed subset of 36 drawn from it (Section II.A, p. 8; Table I, p. 10). The 36 match the size of the original IPCA set, not its variables (footnote 1, p. 4). The main models have FFC6 and three hidden factors, with the intercept either estimated freely or set to zero and the model estimated again (Section II.B, p. 11). A historical comparison covers July 1964 to May 2014 (599 months). The portfolio tests re-estimate every model each March from 2007 to 2025 on the previous 240 months, and form portfolios monthly from March 2007 to November 2025: 225 formation months, with 216 months of returns common to every model (p. 9; Table I, p. 10).


Details

Stocks are split permanently into two groups by a fixed hash of their identifier: the models are learned and the holdings formed on one group (source stocks), and the pricing and hedging tests use portfolios of the other group, the target stocks (p. 9). Each month every characteristic is ranked and centred; missing values enter as zero (p. 9). The three positions studied are book-to-market, momentum (the past eleven months, skipping the latest) and larger-firm size, which takes the larger-firm direction and is not the small-minus-big factor (p. 9; p. 22). Outcomes are the mean excess return and volatility of subsequent monthly returns in bp over 216 common months, before execution and financing costs; mean total position size per dollar of capital over 225 months; and one-way turnover in percent of capital a month over 219 months (Section II.C, pp. 12–13). Intervals come from paired twelve-month calendar blocks. Three separate families of twelve comparisons carry simultaneous 95% intervals (19,999 draws); other intervals are pointwise; all condition on the fitted models (p. 15).

1. Better fit, less representation. With a free intercept, widening the library raises total stock-return R² from 17.01% to 17.70%. The factor part’s relative pricing error (squared average errors over squared average payoffs; lower is better) rises from 76.84% to 92.08% (Table II, p. 17). With the intercept set to zero and the model estimated again, the same error falls from 7.25% to 3.55% instead (p. 16; Table II, p. 17). The larger library adds distinct directions: on average the characteristics behave like 21.08 equally large directions of variation instead of 10.22, a count of stock-exposure directions, not of priced risks (Section IV.A, p. 20).


Figure 2: How much of each familiar position the model’s loadings reproduce, 2007–2025. Coverage, %, at each March estimation date (Figure 3, p. 23).



How to read it. Higher means the loadings reproduce more of the position. Each line is one model (free or zero intercept; 36 or 153 characteristics), re-estimated each March on 240 months; both libraries are measured with the same training-average version of the characteristic ruler. Size is larger-firm positive. Coverage describes stock positions, not return risk or a risk premium. Source: The Ruler Matters, working paper (October 2026), Figure 3; the paper’s figure, reproduced unchanged.



What this shows. The 153-characteristic lines sit below the 36-characteristic lines throughout. With a free intercept, average coverage of momentum falls from 82.27% to 62.33%, and of larger-firm size from 90.17% to 71.93% (p. 22). Not every group falls: intangibles and firm attributes rise from 35.62% to 37.59% (p. 22). Because each position is measured on its own, the fall is an empirical outcome, not a mechanical dilution from adding variables (p. 5; p. 8).

2. Same fit, different credit. Observed and hidden factors can load on the same stocks. With the joint model held fixed, the paper moves the shared part from one block to the other: every fitted return and the joint forecast stay the same; only the split changes (eq. 13, p. 36).


Figure 3: One forecast, three ways to credit it. Mean factor-only forecast contribution, bp a month (Figure IA.2, p. 62).



How to read it. Each panel is one test portfolio. Each group of bars is one convention for crediting the same forecast: coefficient attribution (as estimated), stock-profile attribution (shared exposure reassigned with the characteristic ruler) and return-residual attribution (shared return exposure reassigned to FFC6). Blue bars are the observed factors’ part, grey bars the hidden (latent) factors’ part, and the black dot is their sum. Free intercept, 36 characteristics, averages over 216 months. Source: The Ruler Matters, working paper (October 2026), Internet Appendix, Figure IA.2; the paper’s figure, reproduced unchanged.



What this shows. For larger-firm size, the observed factors’ contribution goes from 1.38 to 45.53 bp a month, and the hidden factors’ from 0.78 to −43.37 bp. Their sum stays at 2.16 bp (Section VII.A, p. 36). A larger reported role for familiar factors can therefore come from how shared exposure is assigned, not from more return variation explained (p. 5). The same holds between the factors and the intercept: reassigning the intercept’s overlap with the loadings gives the factor part relative pricing errors of 53.89% (36) and 72.90% (153), with every fitted return unchanged (p. 16).

3. Same model, different hedge. Hold the model fixed (free intercept, 153 characteristics) and hedge each position at a total position size of one dollar per dollar of capital, once with each ruler (Section V.A, p. 24).


Figure 4: The ruler decides whether a hedge removes the loadings. One model, two rulers, three tilts (Table IA.2, p. 63; Figure IA.3, p. 64).

What this shows. With the plain ruler, 46.10% of a book-to-market hedge and 65.13% of a size hedge still lie on the model’s loadings; the characteristic ruler removes them to numerical precision (Table IA.2, p. 63). That is a difference in how neutral the stocks held are, not a 46.10% cut in variance (p. 6). The two hedges also differ in what follows. For book-to-market, subsequent volatility is 181.03 bp a month under the plain ruler and 83.09 bp under the characteristic ruler. The characteristic-ruler hedge trades more: 18.40% of capital a month, against 13.05% (Table IA.2, p. 63).

4. Keeping the tilt: libraries need different positions. Now restore each position’s original tilt every month and compare the 36- and 153-characteristic models under the loading-neutral hedge (Section V.B, pp. 24–25). With a free intercept, the larger library lowers momentum volatility from 204.26 to 151.25 bp a month, and the mean total position size from 2.34 to 1.62 times capital. For larger-firm size, volatility falls from 275.30 to 152.12 bp, and position size from 3.27 to 1.92 times capital (p. 25). These are separately fitted policies; Table 1 shows how precisely the risk differences are estimated.

What this shows. Only three of the twelve library comparisons have simultaneous intervals that exclude zero: larger-firm size with either intercept, and momentum with a zero intercept (p. 25). With a free intercept, momentum’s −53.00 bp has an interval of [−107.19, 1.19], so the data cannot tell whether its risk fell (p. 25; Table III, p. 27). The hedge rule matters too. 5. Measuring exposure on this month’s stocks. Keep each March’s coefficients for the year, and ask whether this month’s loading correction should be measured on March’s stocks (the annual-origin version of the ruler) or on this month’s (the current version). Both policies hold the same current stocks, keep the same original tilt every month and invest nothing net; only the current version keeps the stocks held neutral to their current loadings through the year (Section VI.B, p. 32).
